The following is a summary of major ship movements and exercises in the Western Pacific over the last week. In Singapore The Theodore Roosevelt Carrier Strike Group pulled into Singapore on Friday for a port visit. The strike group includes aircraft carrier USS Theodore Roosevelt (CVN-71) with embarked carrier air wing (CVW) 11, cruiser USS Chosin (CG-65) and destroyers USS Paul Hamilton (DDG-60) and USS Decatur (DDG-73). Theodore Roosevelt, Chosin and Paul Hamilton docked into Changi Naval Base while Decatur docked into Sembawang. The strike group is expected to transit the Malacca Strait to head to the Middle East following the port visit. Last weekend , the Theodore Roosevelt CSG with fleet oiler USNS Tippecanoe (T-AO-199) carried out cross deck and communication exercises with Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force (JMSDF) destroyer JS Onami (DD-111) in the Philippine and South China seas. In the South China Sea Nimitz-class aircraft carrier USS Theodore Roosevelt (CVN-71) conducts a replenishment-at-sea with Royal Australian Navy Supply-class replenishment oiler HMAS Stalwart (A304), Nov. 4, 2026. US Navy photo Royal Australian Navy fleet oiler HMAS Stalwart (A304) is operating in the South China Sea for the Royal Australian Navy’s regional presence deployment. On Wednesday, aircraft carrier Theodore Roosevelt conducted a replenishment at sea with Stalwart . The U.S. Navy also released a video of the RAS. In the Philippine Sea A graphic posted Nov. 3, 2026, by Joseph Wu, Secretary General of Taiwan’s National Security Council. Taiwan’s National Security Council graphic The Liaoning Carrier Strike Group was operating in the Philippine Sea northeast of Luzon as of Wednesday, according to a graphic posted by Joseph Wu, Secretary General of Taiwan’s National Security Council. The PLAN Liaoning CSG includes aircraft carrier CNS Liaoning (16) cruisers CNS Anshan (101) and CNS Wuxi (104) and destroyer CNS Huainan (123). In Yokosuka, Japan Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force CAPT NAKAZAWA Noriya, commander of Patrol and Defense Squadron 1, Indian Navy Vice Adm. A.N. Pramod, Deputy Chief of Naval Staff, U.S. Navy 7th Fleet Commander Vice Adm. Pat Hannifin, JMSDF CDR YOSHIDA Katsuya, commanding officer of Multi-Mission Stealth Frigate JS Mogami (FFM 1), Royal Australian Navy Rear Adm. Anita Williams, Commander Australian Fleet, and JMSDF Commander in Chief, Self Defense Fleet Vice Adm. OMACHI Katsushi meet aboard Mogami in Yokosuka, Japan during Exercise Malabar 2026, Nov. 5, 2026. US Navy photo The U.S., Japan, Australia and India opened Quad Exercise Malabar 2026 on Thursday with participating ships currently docked in the port for the shore phase of the exercise. The JMSDF is participating with helicopter destroyer JS Ise (DDH-182), frigate JS Mogami (FFM-1), a submarine and a P-1 Maritime Patrol Aircraft for the drills. The Indian Navy deployed frigate INS Sahyadri (F49) and Australia will deploy frigate HMAS Stuart (FFH153) and a Royal Australian Air Force P-8A Poseidon MPA. The U.S. is participating with amphibious transport docks USS Anchorage (LPD-23) and USS John P. Murtha (LPD-26) and a P-8A Poseidon MPA. Anchorage and USS John P. Murtha with amphibious assault ship USS Makin Island (LHD-8) and the embarked 13th Marine Expeditionary Unit form the Makin Island Amphibious Ready Group, which has been docked in Yokosuka for a port visit since Oct. 26. Destroyer USS Ralph Johnson (DDG-114) returned to its homeport of Commander Fleet Activities Yokosuka (CFAY) on Tuesday , according to local ship spotters. In North Korea North Korea conducted a firepower demonstration exercise on Nov. 4, 2026. State media Korea Central News Agency photo North Korea tested its missile strike capabilities Saturday and Monday from undisclosed locations, according to reports by state media Korean Central News Agency (KCNA) . On Saturday, North Korea test fired the Standard Type 2 cluster-bomb warhead for tactical ballistic missiles. On Monday, North Korea tested a strategic cruise missile’s cluster munitions warhead and conducted a vertical strike flight characteristics test. North Korea uses the term “strategic” to denote nuclear weapon capability. North Korea test fired a newly-designed advanced air defense surface-to-air missile and carried out a firepower demonstration exercise with cruise missiles striking a mock airfield target on Wednesday, KCNA reported. South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff said that North Korea fired multiple missiles into the Sea of Japan from the Sondok area. Near South Korea The Republic of Korea Navy Task Fleet Command conducted fleet-level maritime drills in South Korea’s East, West and South Seas from Nov. 1-6, 2026. ROKN photo The Republic of Korea Navy Task Fleet Command conducted fleet-level maritime drills in South Korea’s East, West and South Seas from Sunday to Friday to strengthen the command’s operational capabilities and readiness. The drills include air defense, anti-submarine warfare, anti-surface warfare and the detection and tracking of ballistic missiles with 10 ROKN ships, including destroyers ROKS Yulgok Yi I (DDG-992) and ROKS Jeongjo the Great (DDG-995) and ROKN and Republic of Korea Air Force aircraft. At Jinhae Naval Base, South Korea The Republic of Korea Navy Joint Cruise Training Task Force departed Nov. 3, 2026, from Jinhae. ROKN photo The Republic of Korea Navy Joint Cruise Training Task Force departed Tuesday from Jinhae for a cruise training voyage that will last until Nov. 20 and include port visits to Jeju, South Korea and Guam. The task group includes amphibious assault ship ROKS Marado (LPH-6112), amphibious landing ships ROKS Ilchulbong (LST-688) and ROKS Nojeokbong (LST-689) as well as embarked Republic of Korea Marine Corps MUH-1 Marineon helicopters and 741 second year cadets from three service academies and the Armed Forces Nursing Academy. In Pohang, South Korea The Republic of Korea Marine Corps 1st Marine Division participated in a counter-terrorism and aircraft incident response exercise held at Pohang-Gyeongju Airport on Nov. 4, 2026. ROKMC photo The Republic of Korea Marine Corps 1st Marine Division participated in a counter-terrorism and aircraft incident response exercise held at Pohang-Gyeongju Airport on Wednesday . This year’s exercise involved 15 organizations, including the 1st Marine Division’s counter-terrorism unit, the Korea Airports Corporation, various airlines and local police, fire and medical agencies. The counter terrorism unit conducted a boarding and hostage rescue mission on an airliner in a hijacked aircraft scenario and in a subsequent scenario, a drone carrying explosives that approached the aircraft was jammed and neutralized. “The [Republic of Korea] Marine Corps will continue to strengthen its joint operational capabilities – built upon close coordination with relevant agencies – to respond swiftly and accurately to a wide range of threats,” the ROKMC said. In Kure, Japan Royal Canadian Navy frigate HMCS Regina (FFH334) arrived Nov. 1, 2026, at Kure Naval Base, Japan. JMSDF photo Royal Canadian Navy frigate HMCS Regina (FFH334) arrived Sunday at Kure Naval Base for a port visit. Regina is on deployment under Operation Horizon, the Canadian Armed Forces’ ongoing presence and engagement deployment to the Indo-Pacific. Near Amami Oshima PLAN frigate CNS Jingzhou (532) was sighted Saturday sailing northwest 80 kilometers – 50 miles – northeast of the island of Amami Oshima. The frigate subsequently sailed southwest between Amami Oshima and Yokoate Island to enter the East China Sea. Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force fleet oiler JS Tokiwa (AOE-423) shadowed the PLAN frigate, which previously sailed east through the Osumi Strait between the main island of Kyushi and Tanegashima Island from Oct. 19-20 to enter the Pacific Ocean. In the Miyako Strait Russian Navy surveillance ship Kareliya (535) sailed south between Miyako Island and Okinawa to enter the Philippine Sea on Saturday. The surveillance ship was previously sighted south 50 kilometers – 31 miles – northwest of Kume Island in the East China Sea and subsequently was observed maneuvering northwest and west of Kume Island. JMSDF minesweeper JS Takashima (MSC-603) and a JMSDF P-3C Orion Maritime Patrol Aircraft (MPA) shadowed the Russian ship. Kareliya transited south through the Tsushima Strait from Oct. 27-28 to enter the East China Sea. PLAN destroyer CNS Qiqihar (121) and fast combat support ship CNS Hulunhu (901) on Nov. 1, 2026. Japan Joint Staff Office photo On Sunday, PLAN destroyer CNS Qiqihar (121) and fast combat support ship CNS Hulunhu (901) were sighted sailing northwest 210 kilometers – 130 miles – southeast of Miyako Island and subsequently sailed northwest through the waters between Okinawa and Miyako Island to enter the East China Sea. The two PLAN ships previously sailed east through the Osumi Strait on Oct. 17 to enter the Pacific Ocean. On Monday, Qiqihar and fleet oiler CNS Chaohu (890) were sighted moving southeast 70 kilometers – 43 miles – southwest of Kume Island. Subsequently, the two PLAN ships sailed southeast between Okinawa and Miyako Island to enter the Philippine Sea. A JMSDF P-1 MPA and a JMSDF P-3C Orion MPA carried out surveillance on the PLAN ships. Qiqihar returned Wednesday to the East China Sea, having sailed northwest between Miyako Island and Okinawa. The ship was previously sighted sailing north 130 kilometers – 81 miles – northeast of Miyako Island. A JMSDF Fleet Air Wing 1 P-1 MPA tracked its movements. Chinese UAV flights on Nov. 2, 2026. Japan Joint Staff Office map On Monday, a Chinese WZ-7 reconnaissance Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) flew in from the East China Sea, passing between Okinawa and Miyako Island, to enter the Philippine Sea. The drone carried out circuit flights in the Philippine Sea waters south of Miyako Island to south of Okinawa. The UAV then flew back through the waters between Okinawa and Miyako Island to return to the East China Sea and subsequently headed back to China. A second WZ-7 also flew in from the East China Sea on Monday and flew between Okinawa and Miyako Island to enter the Philippine Sea. The drone carried out circuit flights before returning back the same way to the East China Sea. In response, fighter aircraft from the Japan Air Self-Defense Force’s Southwestern Air Defense Command were scrambled. Near Taiwan On Saturday, a suspected Chinese UAV flew in from the East China Sea and passed between Yonaguni Island and Taiwan to enter the Philippine Sea. Fighter aircraft from the JASDF Southwestern Air Defense Command were scrambled in response. In the East China Sea A Chinese TB-001 reconnaissance UAV in the East China Sea on Nov. 5, 2026. Japan Joint Staff Office photo On Thursday, a Chinese TB-001 reconnaissance UAV flew from China over the East China Sea as far as southwest of the Danjo Islands. The drone subsequently changed course while northwest of Okinawa, and then returned to China. Fighter aircraft from the JASDF Southwestern Air Defense Command were scrambled to intercept the UAV. In La Pérouse Strait Russian Navy cruiser RFS Varyag (011) on Nov. 5, 2026. Japan Joint Staff Office photo Russian Navy cruiser RFS Varyag (011), flagship of the Russian Navy Pacific Fleet, sailed west through La Pérouse Strait, which separates Japan’s main island of Hokkaido from Russia’s Sakhalin Island, to enter the Sea of Japan on Thursday. The cruiser was previously sighted sailing west 40 kilometers – 25 miles – north of Cape Soya, Hokkaido. JMSDF fast attack craft JS Hayabusa (PG-824) and a JMSDF P-1 MPA shadowed the Russian cruiser. In Darwin, Australia Royal Navy ship HMS Tamar prepares to come alongside Kuru Wharf, HMAS Coonawarra, Northern Territory, on Nov. 2, 2026. Australian government photo Royal Navy offshore patrol vessel HMS Tamar (P233) docked Monday at Royal Australian Navy naval base HMAS Coonawarra, Northern Territory to carry out a crew change. Tamar with sister ship HMS Spey (P234) are forward deployed in the Indo-Pacific. This post was written by Dzirhan Mahadzir.

简介 台湾存在战略纵深问题。如果遭到入侵，它没有陆地边界，没有邻国可以撤退，也没有腹地可以争取时间。就台湾而言，在中国登陆后幸存下来的军队和抵抗力量将在地理上受到压缩，并在靠近占领军的地方作战，无处可退。在台湾的情况下，“留守部队”的想法，即那些旨在隐藏、生存并最终在前进的敌人的后方地区行动的部队，即使不是不可能，也是极具挑战性的。该岛的孤立将使得进口武器、医疗用品、外国战士和通讯设备变得困难，即使存在运送这些物品的政治意愿。台湾的地理位置既是抵御入侵的防御资产，也是抵御占领的不利条件。背景信息 在入侵之前规划台湾跨越时空的物理抵抗架构需要创造力。美国的原则在这种情况下提供了丰富的信息，但并不特别适合该岛的独特情况。美国陆军特种部队非常规战争条令，包括野战手册 3-05.201，将“区域综合体”定义为秘密的、分散的设施网络，为抵抗运动提供安全、控制、分散和灵活性，实际上是由抵抗运动本身建立和控制的解放区。
手册建议，该地区综合体应包括安全系统、大本营（这在台湾不太可能，但安全屋是可能且需要的）、通信、后勤、医疗设施、补给库、训练区以及逃生和恢复机制。它将综合体细分为外部和内部安全区，围绕抵抗区指挥部建立，在台湾可能会分散而不是合并。该理论模型假设了连续的、可扩展的地面：抵抗力量可以进入的区域，用于将其外部区域与其内部区域分开，并在到达指挥单元之前吸收压力。台湾可以规划和组织一个内部地带。实际上，它无法建造学说所假设的与它并肩而立的外部世界，因为没有毗邻的领土可以放置它。不幸的是，对于台湾来说，人民是“地理的囚徒”，正如蒂姆·马歇尔的同名著作所暗示的那样。外部安全区有几项工作通常与抵抗组织在同一块土地上进行：组织和发展战士和民事支持基础设施，作为新兵来源，提供第一线的深入安全和警报，并向抵抗组织指挥部提供有关区域内敌方活动的及时、准确的情报。
该区域的成员筛选、选择和训练新的抵抗组织成员，其中最有能力的进入正规武装部队，而与他们并肩建立的文职支援部队则收集情报并向抵抗区域指挥单元提供后勤和心理行动支持。该条令中没有一个假设假设外部区域与其支持的部队隔着开阔的水域。台湾的地理位置迫使我们适应而不是放弃这一概念：志愿者的招募和审查、中国海军通过海峡行动的情报收集，以及对地区指挥单位的后勤和通信支持都发生了变化。这些功能必须在医生允许的距离内执行

【原文 English Original】
Introduction Taiwan has a strategic depth problem. If invaded, it has no land border, no neighboring state to retreat into, and no hinterland to buy time. In the case of Taiwan, military and resistance forces that survive a Chinese landing would be geographically compressed and operating in close proximity to the occupying forces, with nowhere to fall back. The idea of “ stay-behind forces ,” those intended to hide, survive, and eventually operate in the rear area of an advancing enemy, is extremely challenging – if not impossible – in the Taiwan scenario. The island’s isolation would make it difficult to import weapons, medical supplies, foreign fighters, and communications equipment, even where the political will to send them existed. Taiwan’s geography is both a defensive asset against invasion and a liability against occupation. Background Information Planning Taiwan’s physical resistance architecture across time and space, prior to invasion, demands creativity. American doctrine is informative in this case but not particularly well-suited to the island’s one-of-a-kind situation. US Army Special Forces Unconventional Warfare doctrine, including Field Manual 3-05.201 , defines an “area complex” as a clandestine, dispersed network of facilities that gives a resistance movement security, control, dispersion, and flexibility, in effect, a liberated zone built and held by the resistance itself. The manuals recommend that the area complex include a security system, base camps (which will be unlikely in Taiwan, but safehouses will be possible and needed), communications, logistics, medical facilities, supply caches, training areas, and escape and recovery mechanisms. It subdivides the complex into an outer and an inner security zone, built around the resistance area command, which would likely be distributed rather than consolidated in Taiwan. The doctrinal model assumes contiguous, expandable ground: territory a resistance force can grow into, use to separate its outer zone from its inner one, and absorb pressure before it reaches command cells. Taiwan can plan and organize an inner zone. Practically, it cannot build the outer one that doctrine assumes sits alongside it, because there is no adjoining territory to put it in. Unfortunately for Taiwan, the people are “prisoners of geography,” as Tim Marshall’s book of the same name suggests. The outer security zone has several jobs that normally happen on the same landmass as the resistance itself: organizing and developing fighters and civilian support infrastructure, serving as a source of recruits, providing the first line of in-depth security and warning, and feeding the resistance area command cells with timely, accurate intelligence on enemy activity within the zone. Members in that zone screen, select, and train new resistance members, with the most capable moving into the regular armed element, while the civilian support element, built alongside them, gathers intelligence and delivers logistical and psychological operations support to resistance area command cells. None of that doctrine assumes the outer zone sits across open water from the force it supports. Taiwan’s geography forces an adaptation rather than an abandonment of the concept: recruitment and vetting of volunteers, intelligence collection on Chinese naval movements through the straits, and logistics and communications support to area command cells all shift. These functions must be performed at a distance that the doctrine never anticipated. Miyako Strait (Image Credit: The Straits Times) Japan and the Philippines Japan and the Philippines are where the missing outer zone of the area complex can go. In fact, they may be the only realistic locations immediately adjacent to Taiwan that can perform that function. While Guam, Palau, Okinawa, and other places may play a role, the requirement here is to develop locations that can serve as immediate, geographically close extensions of the resistance area complex. Yonaguni Island (Image Credit: South China Morning Post) Both countries are already part of the conversation about a Taiwan contingency, and both have said so in their own words rather than having the role assigned to them by outsiders. Sanae Takaichi, Japan’s Prime Minister, told Japan’s parliament on November 7, 2025, that China’s use of armed force against Taiwan could constitute what Japanese law calls a “survival-threatening situation,” the threshold that permits Japan to exercise collective self-defense. Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. said in August 2025 that a war over Taiwan would draw the Philippines into the conflict regardless of its own preferences, citing proximity and the roughly 180,000 Filipinos residing on the island, and that hope is not a plan. To be clear, neither statement commits either government to a specific military role. The Bashi Channel and Batanes Islands (Image Credit: Robert Luster, StongerNavy.org) Just as geography limits maneuver depth on the island itself, it also narrows where the expanded area complex, depth-by-proxy, could realistically land. Japan’s southwestern Sakishima Islands, particularly Yonaguni, sit 110 kilometers from Taiwan and overlook the Miyako Strait, one of the two principal maritime corridors through which the PLA Navy would seek access to the Western Pacific during a Taiwan conflict. The Philippines’ Batanes Islands sit across the Bashi Channel from Taiwan’s Orchid Island, the second passage , which is 80 kilometers wide . Note that Osumi Strait and Tokara Gap are also available for limited traffic, but for Taiwan operations, the Miyako Strait and Bashi Channel are by far the two principal deep-water exits. Japan is already fortifying Yonaguni with missiles and sensors, while the Philippines has rehearsed rapid anti-ship missile deployments to Batanes during joint exercises with the United States. In addition to the geography requirements of the area complex equation, what is also missing is a special operations mission that’s built to move people, equipment, and information through those same two islands into an occupied Taiwan, and to keep moving them for the resistance once a blockade is in place. Such a mission could include at least four functions. The Resistance Mission The first is communications relay. China has already shown a willingness to sever Taiwan’s connectivity through means short of war: a Chinese-owned vessel was accused of cutting a fiber-optic cable near Keelung Harbor in January 2025, following earlier damage to cables serving Taiwan’s Matsu Islands in 2023. In an actual invasion, isolating Taiwan from the outside world would be an early objective. Relay infrastructure staged on Yonaguni and Batanes, built and rehearsed in peacetime, could keep resistance networks and civilian authorities in contact with the outside world after primary infrastructure fails. The second is unmanned insertion, extraction, and resupply, which helps address the logistics and supply caches that doctrine expects an area complex to maintain internally. Small unmanned surface vessels and unmanned aerial systems, launched at night from Batanes or the Sakishima Islands and running beneath a blockade line, are within current technical reach. This is a mission-planning, basing, and personnel management problem more than a technology problem. Building local relationships, expertise, and staging sites is a peacetime preparation task that retired Special Forces Colonel Brian Petit argued requires a long-dwell, host-embedded advisory presence. Applied to the area-complex concept proposed in this paper, Petit’s idea of a persistent advisory mission adapted to this paper would include US Special Forces not only in Taiwan, but also on the two islands and other locations that would run the resistance pipeline once Taiwan is cut off. An Unmanned Surface Vessel (USV) Penetrates A Chinese Blockade with Ammunition, Medical, and Communication Supplies for The Resistance (Fictional Image. Image Credit: Grok AI) The third is facilitating the introduction of foreign volunteers who want to fight for Taiwan, which supports the doctrinal escape-and-recovery mechanism in reverse: instead of moving evaders out of denied territory, the same tradecraft moves vetted personnel in. Ukraine’s International Legion drew thousands of foreign fighters within weeks of the 2022 Russian invasion, staging through Poland and other neighboring states that were not themselves combatants. Taiwan has no land border and no neighbor that could serve that role by geographic accident. Japan and the Philippines are plausible staging grounds for screening, inserting, and, if necessary, extracting foreign volunteers. A fourth function is kinetic interdiction of Chinese naval forces from Japanese or Philippine soil. This function is more challenging to plan, organize, and train during peacetime because of the obvious political sensitivity. Japan’s “survival-threatening situation” authority and the Philippines’ Mutual Defense Treaty with the United States both provide a legal path to this kind of involvement. But activation would likely occur only once Tokyo or Manila has determined that it is already a party to the conflict and pre-determined thresholds have been crossed. Treating Japan and the Philippines as two more US Special Forces advisory locations alongside Taiwan introduces a harder problem: what sustains a pipeline like this over the years is whether the people running it understand how all three nodes connect, rather than knowing only their own. Not unlike Petit’s concept for Green Berets on long-term Taiwan rotations, a dedicated cadre in this model would instead rotate its personnel sequentially through all three countries, on tours lasting several years each rather than a series of unrelated deployments in which entire teams move in and out at the same time. Optimally, this would include the rotation of not just American advisors but also Japanese, Philippine, and Taiwanese operators. An operator serves a tour in the Philippines, then Japan, then Taiwan, for example, or some ordering suited to the mission, carrying forward what worked in one place and testing it against the next. The result is a body of institutional knowledge about running the resistance pipeline that travels with the people who built it, rather than resetting with every new team that arrives. Foreign Fighters Infiltrate Taiwan to Assist the Resistance (Fictional Image. Image Credit: Google Gemini) Objections Three potential objections to this proposal deserve acknowledgment. The first is consent. Takaichi’s and Marcos’s statements support self-defense and the evacuation of their own nationals. In January 2026, Japan and the Philippines signed a new defense pact amid growing Chinese aggression. Despite this, these actions cannot be interpreted as consent to host an active pipeline built to resupply and reinforce a resistance movement within a state whose government does not formally recognize it. No one should treat public statements from these leaders as a blank check, but the positions from both may serve as a starting point for an expansion of activity. The second is provocation. Beijing’s response to one sentence from Takaichi in the Diet, a halt on Japanese seafood imports , travel advisories, and roughly 500,000 canceled airline tickets , shows how little China needs before retaliating economically. A standing cadre and physical infrastructure on Yonaguni and Batanes will draw an exponentially sharper reaction. The third objection is effectiveness. The Bashi Channel and Miyako Strait are dense, monitored waterways, and unmanned traffic crossing them in wartime will likely be detected and attributed, no matter how careful the tradecraft is, which raises a fair question about whether the pipeline can move enough volume to matter, or perhaps what other functions it may accomplish. Addressing issues related to consent and provocation will be consequential to the success or failure of this proposal. Whether this happens before or after the invasion is also significant. If the Philippines and Japan, or perhaps only one, consider the costs of escalation with China to be borne as a result of embracing this area-complex construct in peacetime, and weigh them against the benefits to be gained for their country in war, they may conclude that the return on investment is worth it. As mentioned earlier, leaders of both countries have articulated that a fight for Taiwan will not be just about Taiwan but will have regional implications, including for their countries. Admittedly, this is not a mitigation of negative costs so much as an acceptance of them. As for the risks associated with establishing communications relay functions and the resistance cadre developing personal relationships on the ground on these adjacent islands, these activities also create similar political and diplomatic costs to those mentioned above. There are genuine, dual-use benefits to establishing communication mechanisms and human-to-human trust networks that come with persistent engagement on these islands, extending beyond conflict or preparation for conflict. Humanitarian Assistance and Disaster Relief preparation, for example, is the most honest example of a capability that would benefit from establishing these systems now. The reality is, however, that building these capabilities prior to invasion may invite retaliation from China. Strategic ambiguity, a constant theme for nearly every country in the world regarding Taiwan, is the first option for the Philippines and Japan as it pursues dual-use preparations discussed here. Or, secondly, both countries may decide to clearly declare their willingness to begin preparing for conflict out of genuine concern for their national security. Or, a third option is that establishing such resistance-support mechanisms may not occur until after hostilities have broken out, and leaders are forced to make hard decisions. The latter outcome doesn’t mean the expanded area complex doesn’t become an operational reality, but it may mean it isn’t optimally planned and exercised. The higher-risk, higher-signature functions involved with the expanded area complex, unmanned insertion runs, and foreign fighter staging become branch plans that would almost certainly not activate until Tokyo or Manila has crossed its own legal thresholds, the same gating already applied to kinetic interdiction. The intent of this paper is not to presuppose what Tokyo or Manila will do or to assume the level of risk these countries are willing to take, but rather to put forth a resistance-support concept and acknowledge the costs associated with it. How these two countries proceed will ultimately be based on what they perceive best for their own survival, not anyone else’s. Effectiveness is a different kind of problem, since it isn’t a matter of managing political risk but of surviving physical detection. There are at least three approaches as to what “success” actually means for this expanded area complex. There is the ambitious one in which the pipeline sustains the resistance movement; the modest one in which the network survives and complicates the enemy’s occupation; and the third, a combination of the two. As for sustaining the resistance itself, it is important to remember that this expanded area complex is the terrestrial-based manifestation of the complex. While the inner and outer zones are where a considerable amount of physical support originates, there will also be maritime (surface and sub-surface), air, space-based, and virtual support to the resistance. Ideally, all of these lines of effort will be well orchestrated. The point here is that it is not only the land-based resistance area complex on Japanese and Philippine islands that will be tasked with supporting the resistance. As for disruption, history provides a useful example. Detachment A, the Cold War Special Forces unit that ran stay-behind operations in West Berlin, never had full deniability, surrounded as it was by Soviet and East German intelligence services, and its value lay in persistence and complication rather than invisibility. This pipeline’s job will include a similar mission: survive attrition and impose cost. In reality, the expanded resistance area complex, together with the other support efforts mentioned, will serve several functions simultaneously. Furthermore, depending on the reality on the ground, one part of the network may serve one function while another serves a different purpose. Summary This paper provides a modern adaptation of the doctrinal “area complex” needed to support resistance on an island facing a realistic threat of invasion and occupation. The overarching strategic concept is outlined here, but the operational and tactical realities of the architecture require additional scrutiny. The idea of a Chinese invasion is often discussed among the US, Taiwan, Japan, the Philippines, and other like-minded partners. The integration of mechanisms across international borders to build depth of resistance to compensate for geographic shortfalls, however, is not explored in practical terms, as it is here. Expanding the area complex’s footprint on the ground is possible if the aperture is spread onto two pieces of partner territory that are not Taiwan’s own. Disclaimer: The views expressed here are the author’s alone and do not reflect the official policy or position of the US Government or the Department of War. The post Expanding Taiwan’s Resistance Area Complex by way of Japan and the Philippines appeared first on Small Wars Journal by Arizona State University .

title: Buy, Don’t Steal: The Economics of Cognitive Warfare
zh_title: 购买，不要偷窃：认知战的经济学
source: Small Wars Journal by Arizona State Univ
summary: 摘要 认知战以个人数据为基础，而美国以低廉的价格出售大部分数据。这篇文章做了三件事：（1）中国为美国选民档案支付的价格； (2) 将其与秘密收集的记录成本进行比较； (3) 提出五项提高对手购买弹药成本的行动。中国购买美国选民数据并不是为了阅读它。它购买了用于瞄准引擎的原材料。商业广告花了二十年的时间来证明，足够大的个人数据池，通过预测模型运行，可以向人们传递不同的、量身定制的信息。
content:
摘要 认知战以个人数据为基础，而美国以低廉的价格出售大部分数据。这篇文章做了三件事：（1）中国为美国选民档案支付的价格； (2) 将其与秘密收集的记录成本进行比较； (3) 提出五项提高对手购买弹药成本的行动。中国购买美国选民数据并不是为了阅读它。它购买了用于瞄准引擎的原材料。商业广告花了二十年的时间来证明，足够大的个人数据池通过预测模型运行，可以向每个人传递不同的、量身定制的信息。将机器指向人们的恐惧和忠诚度而不是购物习惯，其结果就是认知战：通过数据精确地塑造人们的信念和决策方式的竞赛。该杂志的一篇配套文章认为，认知战是基于数据的，因此认知防御是从数据层开始的。这篇文章对那个战场进行了定价。白宫于 2026 年 7 月发布的一份解密记录显示，这些原材料几乎不需要花费任何成本，因为其中大部分都是合法出售的。获取的算术 在早期关于复合战争经济学的著作中，我提出了成本不对称比率，即对手的进攻单位成本除以防御者的反应成本，作为现代冲突中财政消耗的衡量标准。
一架“沙赫德”单向攻击无人机的成本约为 35,000 美元，根据谁的估计，其价格浮动为 15,000 美元，而国会研究服务处定价约为 400 万美元的爱国者拦截机。战略与国际研究中心 (CSIS) 在分析俄罗斯无人机袭击时，采用了同样的 35,000 美元中间值作为故意保守的数字。这种交换比对抗防守者的 100 比 1 更好。在该研究中，14 个典型威胁配对中的 12 个对攻击者有利。解密的材料允许在不同的领域进行相同的分析：情报获取。结果更糟：交易所对攻击者的支持更大。从购买数据的成本开始。美国每个州和哥伦比亚特区都会出售或发布其选民档案。加州将整个文件的费用上限为 100 美元，对于大约 2200 万条记录来说，相当于每个选民的千分之二美分。阿拉巴马州的收费最高，每个名字收费 1 美分，即全州范围内的名单收费约为 38,000 美元。 11 个州根本不收取任何费用，根据选举援助委员会 2020 年编制的数据，24 个州对全州范围内的文件收取 1 至 1,000 美元之间的费用。直接从各州收集的完整国家档案最多可达六位数。中国支付的费用比这个少。
解密文件中最清晰的文件是一份网络防御通知，记录了一名中国行为者于2022年1月从美国商业网站下载了六个州的选民档案，并声明该信息“可从商业网站公开下载”。没有国家费用，没有入侵，没有利用。边际获取成本是带宽和分析师时间。偷窃的成本是多少 这种隐蔽的替代方案有一个价格表，而且这一次是公开的。当司法部于 2025 年 3 月起诉 10 名中国公民代表中国政府进行黑客攻击时，指控文件中描述了承包商 i-Soon 向中国情报机构收取的每个电子邮件费用为 10,000 至 75,000 美元

【原文 English Original】
Abstract Cognitive warfare runs on personal data, and the United States sells much of that data for pennies. This essay does three things: (1) prices what China paid for American voter files; (2) compares that to the documented cost of covert collection; and (3) proposes five actions that raise an adversary’s cost to buy the ammunition. China did not buy American voter data to read it. It bought raw material for a targeting engine. Commercial advertising spent two decades proving that a large enough pool of personal data, run through predictive models, delivers a different, tailored message to each individual. Point that machinery at a population’s fears and loyalties instead of its shopping habits, and the result is cognitive warfare: the contest to shape what a people believes and how it decides, made precise by data. A companion essay in this journal argued that cognitive warfare runs on data, and that cognitive defense therefore begins at the data layer. This essay prices that battlefield. A declassified record that the White House released in July 2026 shows that the raw material cost almost nothing, because most of it was legally for sale. The Arithmetic of Acquisition In earlier work on compound warfare economics, I proposed the Cost Asymmetry Ratio, the adversary’s offensive unit cost divided by the defender’s response cost, as a measure of fiscal attrition in modern conflict. A Shahed one-way attack drone costs roughly $35,000, give or take $15,000 depending on whose estimate one credits, and forces a Patriot interceptor that the Congressional Research Service prices at roughly $4 million. The Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) adopted that same $35,000 midpoint as a deliberately conservative figure when analyzing Russian drone strikes. The exchange runs better than 100-to-1 against the defender. In that study, 12 of 14 canonical threat pairings favor the attacker. The declassified materials permit the same analysis in a different domain: intelligence acquisition. The results are worse: the exchange favors the attacker by an even wider margin. Start with what the data costs to buy. Every US state and the District of Columbia sells or releases its voter file. California caps the fee for its entire file at $100, which for roughly 22 million records works out to about a two-thousandth of a cent per voter. Alabama, at the expensive end, charges one cent per name, or roughly $38,000 for its statewide list. Eleven states charge nothing at all, and according to Election Assistance Commission data compiled in 2020, 24 states charged between $1 and $1,000 for a statewide file. A complete national file assembled directly from the states runs to the low six figures at most. China paid less than that. The clearest document in the declassified release, a network-defense notice , records a Chinese actor downloading the voter files of six states from US commercial websites in January 2022 and states that the information “is publicly available for download from the commercial websites.” No state fee, no intrusion, no exploit. The marginal acquisition cost was bandwidth and analyst hours. What Stealing Costs The covert alternative has a price list, and for once it is public. When the Justice Department indicted 10 Chinese nationals in March 2025 for hacking on behalf of the Chinese government, the charging documents described the contractor i-Soon billing Chinese intelligence services between $10,000 and $75,000 for each email inbox it successfully compromised, with further payments for analyzing the contents. Leaked internal files from the same company, analyzed by SentinelOne in 2024, show data from a foreign ministry fetching roughly $55,000. i-Soon employed over 100 people and projected revenues near $75 million. Those are the discount rates for soft targets, accounts and networks protected by ordinary commercial security. Hard targets are devices and systems that can only be breached with novel unpublished exploits. The exploit brokers that supply state programs publish their bids: up to $7 million for a full-chain iPhone compromise, $5 million for Android. RAND’s study of zero-day vulnerabilities found a median useful life near seven years, which is the asset an intelligence service burns when an operation is discovered. Above all of it sits a national intelligence budget the Director of National Intelligence discloses only as a top line, $73.4 billion requested for fiscal 2025, with everything below that classified. Set the routes side by side. Ten thousand dollars per inbox is the cheapest documented rate for stealing personal data one target at a time. One hundred dollars buys the registration record of every voter in California. The asymmetry is three to four orders of magnitude in direct cost, and that is before risk is priced at all. Covert collection carries indictment, attribution, sanctions, and the loss of tools that took years to build. A commercial download carries none. The defender’s side of the ratio is worse still. Equifax agreed to a settlement of at least $575 million and potentially $700 million for a breach affecting 147 million people. UnitedHealth Group reported that the Change Healthcare attack would cost roughly $2.87 billion in 2024. A breach of the Office of Personnel Management compromised background investigation files on 21.5 million people, including 5.6 million sets of fingerprints, at a national security cost no settlement figure captures. On the kinetic battlefield, an attacker spends a dollar to force thousands. In the data domain, the attacker spends nothing to force billions, or, when the data is legally public, to force no response at all, because there is nothing to remediate and no one to indict. The Portfolio Is the Tell The declassified catalog of data held by a People’s Republic of China computer network exploitation actor around 2019 reads as my cost-asymmetry framework predicts. Most of its American entries are cheap or free: voter files, breached credentials circulating in criminal dumps, social media account data, the commodity substrate of identity resolution. A small number of entries fall into a different category: F-15 maintenance and technical manuals, and documents from four cleared defense contractors. Technical data tied to items on the United States Munitions List cannot be bought at any price, which is precisely why it was stolen. That split is what a rational collector produces. Commodity data is purchased or scraped because covert action against it would be economically irrational. Export-controlled technical data is stolen because no legal market exists. Expensive, risky tradecraft is reserved for the material money cannot buy. An intelligence service that behaves this way is optimizing, and the results of that optimization are reflected in the price column. This reframes how the July release should be read. The alarming interpretation, that a 2022 download of public records constitutes an election compromise, misprices the event. The economic interpretation is more troubling: the United States has structured its data environment so that the cheapest route to a national targeting file on the American population runs through lawful commerce. The vulnerability is not a firewall. It is a fee schedule. Why the Cheapest Input Buys the Most Influence Cognitive warfare is the effort to shape a population’s perceptions, judgments, and decisions. Congress ordered the Department of War to define it in the 2026 National Defense Authorization Act , a task still unfinished months past its deadline, and this journal has carried a sustained debate over whether the term describes anything new. Set the doctrinal argument aside, and the mechanism is one the advertising industry already built. Gather enough data on a person, model what moves them, and serve a message calibrated to that individual. Advertising technology runs this logic billions of times a day to sell products. A state with the same pool of data does it to sell doubt and division, one citizen at a time, and adversaries are already contesting that space with AI-generated content at scale. The declassified materials indicate that China reasons this way. Beside the voter files sits a plan to exploit American fault lines over race, immigration, and the pandemic response, and to push tailored narratives through social and traditional media. Traditional propaganda involves broadcasting one message to everyone and hoping it lands. A data-driven campaign delivers a different message to each person, measures who responds, and adjusts. The difference is the objective. A retailer wants a purchase. An adversary wants a belief. Here the implications for scale turn the economics from severe to alarming. A broadcast’s reach is capped by its cost. A data-driven influence campaign’s is not, because once the pool of data exists, the marginal cost of one more tailored message approaches zero. China assembled that pool for pennies. The input to one of the most consequential forms of modern influence, the shaping of a democratic population’s decisions, is the cheapest item on the battlefield. Inverting the Curve In the kinetic domain, the fix for a bad exchange ratio is a cheaper defense: a laser shot costing a few dollars against a drone costing tens of thousands. The data domain has an analog, and it is regulatory, not technical. Executive Order 14117 and the Justice Department’s Data Security Program , in force since April 2025, function as an export control on Americans’ bulk sensitive data, restricting transfers to six countries of concern. The economic effect is the point. The rule raises the adversary’s acquisition cost at the cheapest point on the curve, the legal purchase, and pushes collection back toward the covert route, where cost, risk, and attribution all favor the defender. A dollar of acquisition cost imposed at the point of sale buys more security than a dollar of breach response after the loss. From Arithmetic to Action: Five Recommendations Five actions raise the adversary’s cost to acquire the ammunition of cognitive warfare. First, extend and enforce the bulk-data transfer restrictions. Close the reseller and aggregation seams through which restricted categories leak, and fund the enforcement capacity to detect violations, since an unenforced export control prices at zero. Second, reprice public records for bulk machine access. This does not require closing them. Transparency for citizens, journalists, campaigns, and researchers can coexist with fees, identity verification, and rate limits calibrated to make wholesale foreign harvesting expensive and visible. A journalist checking a voter roll and a foreign actor downloading 51 jurisdictions are different acts, and the fee schedule should treat them differently. Third, harden the holders whose data cannot be bought. As the legal route closes, adversary covert spending will concentrate on cleared defense contractors, health systems, and genomic repositories. Security investment should follow that predicted shift rather than trail it. Fourth, extend acquisition-cost logic to minors’ data. Behavioral and biometric profiles built on children age into profiles of cleared analysts and field-grade officers, which makes children’s data the longest-dated asset in an adversary’s portfolio and the least defended. Fifth, measure defense by the adversary’s cost to acquire. Program evaluation across data security, foreign investment review, and privacy enforcement should report the acquisition cost imposed on a hostile collector, because that figure, rather than defender spending, predicts adversary behavior. The Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States ( CFIUS ) and Federal Trade Commission children’s-privacy enforcement already generate the underlying data. Deterrence here comes from arithmetic, as it does against drones: make the cost to acquire this data exceed the influence it buys. Raising that cost is not only privacy protection, or even counterintelligence. It denies easy access to the ammunition needed for the fight over what Americans believe. Today the price runs in the opposite direction by orders of magnitude, and the adversary reads the price list as easily as we do. The cheapest weapon in the arsenal is the one aimed between our ears. A Note on Estimates and Sources Voter file figures are drawn from published state fee schedules; the national-assembly range is an inference, not an audited total. Covert collection prices are drawn from the March 2025 Justice Department indictment and from analysis of leaked contractor files. Remediation figures come from Federal Trade Commission settlement documents and Securities and Exchange Commission filings. The Cost Asymmetry Ratio framework is developed in The Cost Curve as Deterrent, with the simulator and data sources on GitHub. Disclaimer: The views expressed are the author’s own. The post Buy, Don’t Steal: The Economics of Cognitive Warfare appeared first on Small Wars Journal by Arizona State University .

title: 影音筆記：台灣選舉漫遊
summary: 臨近台灣地方大選，我們製作了一部《台灣選舉漫遊錄》，走訪台北、高雄、花蓮和新竹，看看這些地方的政治，和選舉版圖背後沒說的故事。 高雄美濃和台北大稻埕，一個是南部的客家庄，一個是台北最老的街區之一。如果只看選舉結果，這兩個地方幾乎站在光譜的兩端：美濃常被說是藍綠五五波，或稍微偏向國民黨（藍營）的地方；大稻埕所在的大同區，則是不少人口中的民進黨（綠營）大本營。 整理影片素材時，我發現這些散落的訪談片段，好像都在繞著同一個問題打轉：一個人，是怎麼開始在乎一個地方的？ 2026年10
content: 臨近台灣地方大選，我們製作了一部《台灣選舉漫遊錄》，走訪台北、高雄、花蓮和新竹，看看這些地方的政治，和選舉版圖背後沒說的故事。 高雄美濃和台北大稻埕，一個是南部的客家庄，一個是台北最老的街區之一。如果只看選舉結果，這兩個地方幾乎站在光譜的兩端：美濃常被說是藍綠五五波，或稍微偏向國民黨（藍營）的地方；大稻埕所在的大同區，則是不少人口中的民進黨（綠營）大本營。 整理影片素材時，我發現這些散落的訪談片段，好像都在繞著同一個問題打轉：一個人，是怎麼開始在乎一個地方的？ 2026年10月22日，高雄美濃。攝：陳焯煇/端傳媒 讀報的人 在美濃，幾乎每位受訪者都不約而同提到一件事：這裡的書香氣息。 返鄉青年小汶記得，每天都會有一份報紙送到家，爺爺看完不多說什麼，但都整整齊齊地把報紙疊好；在美濃國中教了二十多年書的橘子老師則說，她剛嫁來時最驚訝的，是眼睛已經看不太清楚的老阿伯，還每天在看報紙。 「他們都建構了一段自己的中心思想。」橘子老師說，即使是農民，對農業也有自己的見解。也難怪美濃的協會多得驚人，有腳踏車協會、八色鳥協會、各地的同鄉會，還有能展現在地文化氣質的「博士學人會」。在橘子老師的故鄉，大家遇到困難，常常是抱怨完就結束了，但美濃不一樣，抱怨完會開會，開完會就行動。 聽到這裡，我忍不住想：藍綠能在這裡打成平盤，會不會就是這樣來的？一個大家都讀、都想、都能獨立思考的地方，本來就很難被一種聲音帶著走。 小汶說，長輩在三合院裡聊政治，從來不趕小孩走，也不搞一言堂。自己家裡多是支持民進黨的聲音，但她能在國中同學口中聽到「家裡要投馬英九」，理由是「因為他比較帥」。小汶回家轉述，大人也只是笑一笑，沒有人說誰對誰錯。那是她第一次意識到，原來投票不一定要跟著政黨走，也可以是因為「這個人」。 這種選人不選黨的習慣，到現在也沒變。小汶說，對美濃人而言，重點往往不是你代表哪一黨，而是你的政見裡有沒有美濃。想出來選里長？你得先問問左右五戶鄰居認不認識你。 當然，這只是我的假設，五五波的背後還有人口結構、產業、地方派系等許多成因。但「讀得多、想得多」這件事，或許讓這裡的政治分歧相對健康，而不針鋒相對。橘子老師說，美濃人之間的政治立場不同，但大家都會守住那條界線。你的容忍度高，我們就多聊，說不定可以互相說服；你的容忍度低，我們就各退一步，不聊政治。 瓦豆燈光創辦人江佶洋。攝：陳焯煇/端傳媒 上街的人 「沒有學識，你是不會上街的。」這句話，是在大稻埕聽到的。 瓦豆燈光老闆的同學曾經批評，上街頭的都是沒讀書、知識水平低的人。老闆的反駁很直接：連吃飽都有問題的人，根本不會上街頭。一定是先有人提出論述、有想法、有號召力，才會有人跟上。 他自己就是這樣長大的。在那個沒有網路、沒有通訊軟體的年代，鄭南榕的《自由時代》是他們家的課外讀物，集會的消息就登在上面；就算無法取得這樣的「非法刊物」，其實鄰里之間也會互通集會遊行的訊息。一家人吃完飯，參加政見發表會、遊行抗議，都是很稀鬆平常的事。 雖然老闆是從在地經驗、陣營視角出發，但我聽著聽著，想到的卻是美濃。反水庫運動、黃蝶祭，以及前面一長串的協會和同鄉會，美濃蓬勃的社會參與背後，不也是一群讀報、讀書、有自己見解的人嗎？ 所以當有人選擇走上街頭時，我們或許不該急著把他們定性成被煽動、暴動。願意開口說的、勇於走上街的、甚至為此付出龐大代價的，往往是在心裡想過很多遍的人。 懷抱希望的人 瓦豆老闆還分享了一個有趣的觀察。早年的造勢場合，音樂一放就是〈黃昏的故鄉〉，「悲情」往往是活動的主旋律。直到 1994 年陳水扁參選台北市長，第一次用「快樂、希望」作為訴求。 他就這樣看了四十年，看著民進黨的競選歌曲從〈春天的花蕊〉、〈伊是咱的寶貝〉到〈自信勇敢咱的名〉，一次比一次好聽、街頭一次比一次像嘉年華。老闆說，那是一個民族開始站起來的樣子。 聽到這裡，老闆眼中泛著的欣慰讓我深受感動。悲情動員有它的歷史，那些傷痛也都是真的，但正是我們願意正視，能公平、公開地討論這段歷史，後來的人才能放下一點重量，帶著社會往前走。一個社會走得夠遠了，我們或許才能用希望，而不只是恐懼、仇恨來凝聚彼此。 不論是哪次選舉、哪個陣營，希望候選人都能帶領選民，一起想像地方的未來，而不只是攻擊對手、情緒動員。 大稻埕開咖啡館的盧郭老闆。攝：陳焯煇/端傳媒 收集故事的人 這一集，我們原本想拍的是選舉，但最後拍到的，反而是一部收集故事的漫遊錄。 在大稻埕開咖啡館的盧郭老闆是深綠支持者。他講起自己高中時讀到民主前輩們的故事，說了一句很沉重的話：「你知道了，就很難回去了。」 回頭看這兩個地方，我想「知道」大概就是一切的起點。知道這塊土地擁有什麼、發生過什麼，人才會開始在乎它。 但光是在乎還不夠，還得知道該怎麼做。在美濃，當年參與反水庫運動的作詞人鍾永豐，也把如何組織、如何跟政府溝通的經驗分享給下一代；瓦豆老闆則記得，開票那晚，爸媽會和鄰居約好每人帶一支手電筒到開票所，怕有人會製造停電、做票。 這些「知道」都不是課本教的，而是長輩一次次上街、一次次在餐桌上說給下一代聽的。 也難怪瓦豆老闆一直拜託身邊的人要讀文學、讀歷史。因為不讀，就沒辦法對下一代講故事，也感受不到今天能自由參與政治，背後有多少重量。 所以不管是美濃的五五波，還是大稻埕的一片綠，人們選擇的方向不同，在乎的方式也不同，但都是先知道了、想過了，才決定站出來。就像盧郭老闆說的，一旦知道了，就很難再回去了。 下一集，我們將帶著你們前往花蓮、新竹。看看一個人口嚴重外流的地方，和人口大量移入的城市，他們會出現怎麼樣的政治差異。

title: US Air Force eyes reviving WWII air bases in the Pacific
zh_title: 美国空军着眼于复兴太平洋地区的二战空军基地
summary: 据美国空军部发布的公告称，美国空军希望每年在西北太平洋三个美国岛屿上的四个机场执行超过 6000 架次的飞机行动，其中包括一个正在翻新的二战时期主要机场。该部门发布了一份准备环境影响报告的意向通知，该报告将评估塞班国际机场、天宁岛国际机场、天宁岛北机场和罗塔国际机场的培训和运营的“潜在社会、经济和环境影响”。岛屿
content:
据美国空军部发布的公告称，美国空军希望每年在西北太平洋三个美国岛屿上的四个机场执行超过 6000 架次的飞机行动，其中包括一个正在翻新的二战时期主要机场。该部门发布了一份准备环境影响报告的意向通知，该报告将评估塞班国际机场、天宁岛国际机场、天宁岛北机场和罗塔国际机场的培训和运营的“潜在社会、经济和环境影响”。这些岛屿是北马里亚纳群岛联邦的一部分，是美国的非建制领土。拟议的训练和演习将支持空军的敏捷作战作战概念，该概念强调部队在机场之间的分散以及在各种条件下维持作战的同时在机场之间进行机动的能力，目的是挫败对手通过瞄准单个基地来关闭这些作战的能力。众所周知，ACE 的发展很大程度上是为了应对中国军队不断扩大的影响力和不断扩大的导弹库。
通知称，这四个机场为支持 ACE 提供了“独特的机会”，其基础设施从“完全开发的商业机场到远征作战地点”各不相同。这三个岛屿彼此相距不到几十海里，这将允许进行反映分布式行动复杂性的训练，同时减少它们之间的运输时间。它们距离美国另一个领土关岛的主要军事基地以北不到100海里，该基地将为这些演习提供部队的集结和部署。通知中写道，这三个机场“共同提供了一个训练环境，使[空军]能够进行分布式作战、测试和使用可定制的部队包、加强保障和机动能力以及增强作战弹性”。环境影响报告将评估拟议活动的潜在影响，其中包括每年举行几次、每次为期几周的小型、中型和大型训练和演习，包括每年在每个机场进行多达 1,200 次固定翼和 320 次旋转翼操作，例如起飞和着陆。
它还将评估替代方案，即每个机场每年最多进行 1,400 次固定翼飞机和 384 次旋转翼飞机运行，以及“无行动替代方案”。训练和演习将由每个机场最多 550,000 加仑的燃料、每个机场最多 1,000 名人员、远征基础设施的临时安装、箔条和照明弹等弹药的处理以及支持服务以及训练和演习前后的活动提供支持。拟议的活动是在经过数年的升级相关机场的工作之后进行的，特别是天宁岛的机场，这些机场是在第二次世界大战。北机场在战后处于闲置状态，在 2023 年底开始修复工作时，大部分被植被覆盖。空军还升级了港口和道路基础设施、燃料管道和机场表面以及公用设施，以促进天宁岛的扩大行动。机场修复工作引起了空军领导人对资源和资金的一些疑问，特别是在与伊朗的战争提出了新的要求的情况下

【原文 English Original】
The U.S. Air Force hopes to conduct more than 6,000 aircraft operations annually at four airfields on three American islands in the northwest Pacific Ocean, including a major WWII-era airfield that is being refurbished , according to an announcement from the Department of the Air Force. The department published a notice of intent to prepare an environmental impact statement that will assess “potential social, economic, and environmental effects” of training and operations at Saipan International Airport, Tinian International Airport, Tinian North Field and Rota International Airport. The islands are part of the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands, an unincorporated U.S. territory. The proposed training and exercises will support the Air Force’s Agile Combat Operations concept, which emphasizes dispersal of forces across airfields and the ability to maneuver between them while sustaining operations under a range of conditions, with the goal of thwarting an adversary’s ability to shut down those operations by targeting a single base. ACE, as it’s known, has developed largely in response to the Chinese military’s growing reach and expanding missile arsenal.  The notice said the four airfields provide “a unique opportunity” to support ACE, with infrastructure that varies from “fully developed commercial airfields to expeditionary operating locations.” The three islands are within a few dozen nautical miles of each other, which would allow for training that reflects the complexity of distributed operations while reducing transit time between them. They are less than 100 nautical miles north of the major military bases on Guam, another U.S. territory, which would support the staging and deployment of forces for those exercises. The three airfields “collectively provide a training environment that enables [the Air Force] to exercise distributed operations, test and employ tailorable force packages, strengthen sustainment and maneuver capabilities, and enhance operational resilience,” the notice reads. The environmental impact statement will evaluate the potential effects of the proposed activities, which include small, medium and large trainings and exercises held several times a year for a few weeks at a time and consisting of up to 1,200 fixed-wing and 320 rotary-wing operations, like takeoffs and landings, annually at each airfield. It will also assess an alternative scenario with up to 1,400 fixed-wing and 384 rotary-wing operations per airfield annually and a “No Action Alternative.” The trainings and exercises would be supported by up to 550,000 gallons of fuel at each airfield, up to 1,000 personnel per airfield, the temporary installation of expeditionary infrastructure, the handling of munitions like chaff and flares, as well as support services and pre-and post-training and exercise activities.  The proposed activity comes after several years of work to upgrade the airfields in question, especially the airfields on Tinian, which were built and heavily used during WWII. North Field was inactive after the war and was largely covered with vegetation when the rehabilitation effort began in late 2023. The Air Force also upgraded port and roadway infrastructure, fuel pipelines and airfield surfaces, and utilities to facilitate expanded operations on Tinian . The airfield rehabilitation efforts have created some questions among Air Force leaders about resourcing and funding, particularly as the war with Iran has placed new demands on the force. Island residents also have misgivings about the projects. While some welcome the investment that the construction and military operations will bring, others have doubts that the increased activity will really benefit the islands’ populations and that the Pentagon will be transparent about its activity and responsive to local concerns.  The Department of the Air Force will hold public meetings this month on Saipan, Tinian and Rota to get feedback on the proposal, with written comments due by Nov. 29. The department plans to produce a draft environmental impact statement for public comment in fall 2027 and a final version in mid-2028.

title: 台湾：支持美光工人罢工
source: 中国劳工论坛 China Worker
summary: 这场斗争也是全体工人的斗争 陈延年 国际社会主义道路（ISA）台湾 10月7日，台湾美光晶圆科技企业工会（桃园工会）正式发布罢工投票结果。在全体会员高达89.1%的高参与率下，工会以高达99.1%的压倒性同意率正式取得合法罢工权。这不仅是美光建厂以来的首次，更是台湾半导体与高科技产业史上的首例合法罢工授权事件，并已正式宣布于10月22日（周四）发动为期一天的首波实际罢工行动，以声援会员人数已增至11,000人（覆蓋率近90%）的台中工会。 美光正如许多跨国资本，只是与其他科技
content: 这场斗争也是全体工人的斗争 陈延年 国际社会主义道路（ISA）台湾 10月7日，台湾美光晶圆科技企业工会（桃园工会）正式发布罢工投票结果。在全体会员高达89.1%的高参与率下，工会以高达99.1%的压倒性同意率正式取得合法罢工权。这不仅是美光建厂以来的首次，更是台湾半导体与高科技产业史上的首例合法罢工授权事件，并已正式宣布于10月22日（周四）发动为期一天的首波实际罢工行动，以声援会员人数已增至11,000人（覆蓋率近90%）的台中工会。 美光正如许多跨国资本，只是与其他科技巨头比赛谁能从劳工身上榨取最多血汗。当前会发起罢工不是没有原因的。随着生成式AI爆发，美光在高频宽记忆体（HBM）与高阶DRAM等领域赚取了暴利，最新2026会计年度（FY2026）财报显示全年营收冲上1,332亿美元历史纪录，且2027年全年HBM高阶产能早已被客户预订一空。 基层劳工被压榨 然而，2023年记忆体寒冬期间，台湾厂区即便仍有获利，基层劳工却依然遭到美光总公司要求齐头式裁员10%并全面冻结奖金。如今面对公司的空前荣景，底薪与分红却被刻意压制。资方将高阶主管与基层员工的薪酬差距拉大到令人发指的地步：2025年美光全年净利暴增逾10倍达85亿美元，但黑箱的IPP绩效奖金制度却仅给出93.9%的达成率系数（「勿忘93.9」），台湾员工实际领取的绩效奖金仅约2.6个月薪资，而执行长的年度现金绩效奖励却高达32.4个月！ 在2025年限制型股票奖励（RSA）分配上，全球员工平均仅获约207股，执行长却得83,015股，差距高达400倍（2023年亏损裁员期间差距更达570倍）！而台湾员工在限制型股票单位（RSU）的覆蓋率过往更仅有约40%，远低于美国厂区的近100%。劳工多年付出的心血遭到资方高层无情地窃取。 美光的南韩竞争对手如三星电子与SK海力士，在面临强大工会罢工威胁后，皆已将年度营业利益的10.5%至12%（三星）与10%（SK海力士）明确化作为分润基础。反观台湾美光，资方却拒绝建立透明的「营业利益15%常态化按季分润制」，反而在9月11日未经协商片面宣布每人100万新台币的「一次性感谢金」，并以基层作业员约3万元的极低底薪为分母，包装出「整体薪酬最高68个月」的公关话术（月薪6万元者实领折算仅约25.45个月），实质新增奖酬仅占公司营业利益约4.4%，企图以此收买基层、瓦解罢工动能。 资方之所以敢如此傲慢，实际上是因为台湾长期缺乏足以迫使科技资本家低头的强大工会运动。台湾美光约15,000名员工仅占全球逾6万名人力约四分之一，却贡献了全球高达50%～60%以上的DRAM与先进记忆体产能。这一切丰厚利润与晶圆产出，明明都是工人血汗劳动与日夜轮班的结晶，如今管理层却向华尔街承诺在扣除资本支出后，将100%超额自由现金流全数用于扩大库藏股回购以回馈股东与推升股价，沦为华尔街与高层予取予求的禁脔。 「摸头妥协」 资方在先前的劳资协商中毫无诚意，多次将决策推托给10月8日至9日召开的美国总公司董事会；然而董事会结束已超过10天，资方仍未针对分润金额与制度提出任何具体对案，仅以「48周年餐食补助」与缺货的「PayEasy礼品」敷衍塞责。10月15日美光台中先进封装测试二厂（AATT2）启用时，美光全球营运长甚至完全避谈罢工争议。 然而，10月21日台湾美光与台中工会突袭发布联合声明，宣布双方已正式签署劳资协议，并撤回原订22日的调解程序。美光所谓的2027会计年度新薪酬制度，不仅将季度利润奖金强制拆分为「50%现金、50%须锁闭一年归属的股票」，更在奖金池计算中埋下陷阱：规定每季必须「先扣除／预留下一季资本支出所需资金」后，才计算员工利润奖金，且未透明公开获利提拨比例公式。这根本是把公司疯狂扩厂的财务压力，直接转嫁到员工的奖金池。当基层奖金被压缩的同时，美国高层和华尔街股东却靠着公司买回库藏股、拉抬股价，继续爽领巨额利润！而原先工会要求的今年度一次性大额现金补偿与四大诉求则全数落空。 这起未经民主程序、未公开协议文本、更未经会员大会投票表决的「摸头妥协」，引爆台中工会内部1.1万名基层会员的愤慨。基层劳工痛批：「四大诉求一个都没有达到怎么会妥协？成员对内容完全不知情，也没有带回来民主投票！」面对干部以「明天开奖就知道为什么够了」敷衍，会员已发起线上紧急连署，要求撤销原签约授权、完整公开最终文本，并依《工会法》门槛要求召开临时会员大会重新审议。 绝不接受背叛 更有甚者，台中工会干部在21日单独与资方签约撤回调解，不仅背弃了此前与桃园工会「双厂同进退、共同列席谈判」的盟约，更让已握有罢工权、准备在22日发动一日警告性罢工以声援台中的桃园工会陷入孤立。而美光台湾将桃园与台中登记为两家独立公司法人的壁垒，让资方有空间分流谈判，又遭到少数干部在保密条款下「先斩后奏」地代表签约，这些都暴露出资方借由分化个别厂场工会、以不透明协议试图瓦解劳动阶级团结的惯用伎俩。这场突如其来的妥协风波，再次血淋淋地证明资本家绝不会自动施舍，而官僚化的密室协商更只会出卖工人的血汗成果。■ 国际社会主义道路主张： 支持台中美光基层会员行使民主权利，坚决拒绝保密黑箱！声援台中厂会员发起的连署行动，要求立即公开劳资协议最终文本，并召开临时会员大会进行实质审议与民主投票；反对少数干部在密室中代表超过一万名成员签署协议。 支持桃园工会的罢工抗争，两厂工人应拒绝被各个击破！针对资方刻意利用法人壁垒与各厂协商时间差进行的分化，我们呼吁桃园工会继续捍卫基层权益，同时支援台中工会会员打破黑箱；工人的权利必须靠集体动员与公开透明的争取，拒绝打了折扣的摸头方案。 建设民主决策、积极斗争的工会组织！各厂工会干部必须受到全体会员民主授权与罢免权的严格监督。同时保护罢工工人与工会干部不被资方秋后算帐，阻止资方在AI泡沫破裂时要工人承担苦果。 动员群众集会，桃园与台中两厂工人应共同讨论并投票制定运动的下一步。并协调跨企业的工人共同行动，串联台积电等半导体产业劳工，打破资方的工会禁令组织团结斗争，不被老板们各个击破，共同对抗台湾高科技业普遍长工时与分红不透明的剥削。 建设群众斗争，打破台湾现有反民主亲资方的工会组织门槛、政治罢工禁令与跨企业联合罢工限制。支持国际工人发起协调斗争，连结美光全球各厂区以及南韩三星、SK海力士等的跨国科技工人，反对资方任何企图分化、差别对待不同国籍劳工的手段。 這篇文章 台湾：支持美光工人罢工 最早出現於 中国劳工论坛 China Worker 。

title: Bank of England pours cold water on AI productivity boom
zh_title: 英格兰银行给人工智能生产力繁荣泼冷水

content:
英国央行表示，尽管在人工智能领域投入了数十亿美元，但该技术并没有为英国企业带来生产力的提高。在最新的货币政策报告中，央行发现过去三年人工智能使英国生产力提高了约 0.5%。这意味着自 2024 年初以来，年生产率仅额外增长 0.1 至 0.2 个百分点，这远不是硅谷所希望的经济革命。英国央行表示：“人工智能投资似乎对当前的需求强劲做出了一定贡献，但到目前为止，只有证据表明人工智能推动了英国生产率增长的适度增长。”即使是被认为最有可能从这项技术中受益的行业也没有什么值得夸耀的。信息和通信等人工智能密集型行业的生产率增长有所改善，但尚未超过大流行前的平均水平。这并不是说人工智能没有为英国经济做任何事情。该银行估计，自 2026 年初以来，人工智能相关活动占英国 GDP 增长的近五分之一，尽管其中大部分似乎来自开发和部署该技术的公司，而不是通过使用该技术提高生产力的企业。
报告称：“迄今为止，人工智能对经济增长的贡献似乎反映了人工智能技术上游开发和实施的活动，而不是在经济其他领域采用人工智能技术所带来的更广泛的收益。”换句话说，事实证明，销售人工智能比实际使用它更有利可图。该银行还警告称，不要将英国近期生产率提高的功劳过多地归功于人工智能。增长的主要原因似乎是企业雇用的工人减少了，而产出却持续增长，部分原因是企业放松了大流行后的人员配置决定并应对更高的就业成本。尽管预测人工智能将导致大量劳动力失业，但接受世行决策者小组调查的公司报告称，迄今为止对就业几乎没有总体影响。然而，这项技术使得一些雇主不太愿意雇用新员工或替换离职员工。其他研究表明，企业仍在等待回报。 Gartner 上个月发布的一项调查发现，虽然四分之三的企业董事会成员期望人工智能能够提高生产力并削减成本，但只有 3% 的组织实际上实现了目标。与此同时，38% 的人在人工智能方面的支出已经超出预算，但 85% 的人计划明年支出更多。
2 月份发布的另一项涉及近 6,000 名高管的研究发现，超过 80% 的公司没有看到人工智能对就业或生产力产生明显影响。显然，解决令人失望的回报的答案是继续写支票。人工智能支出与实际回报之间日益脱节也引起了金融监管机构的注意。国际货币基金组织上个月警告称，如果承诺的利润没有兑现，人工智能支出热潮可能会再次给投资者带来损失，并可能拖累更广泛的经济。国际清算银行 (Bank for International Settlements) 在 6 月份发出了类似的警报，将当前的支出热潮与 20 世纪 90 年代的互联网泡沫进行了比较。它担心的是，科技巨头正在向基础设施投入巨额资金，因为他们假设人工智能最终将带来同样巨大的回报，例如

【原文 English Original】
Despite the billions being thrown at artificial intelligence, the technology has delivered little in the way of productivity gains for UK businesses, according to the Bank of England. In its latest Monetary Policy Report , the central bank found that AI has increased UK productivity by an estimated 0.5 percent over the past three years. That works out to just 0.1 to 0.2 percentage points of additional annual productivity growth since early 2024, hardly the economic revolution Silicon Valley has been promising. "AI investment appears to be contributing somewhat to current demand strength, but so far there is only evidence of a modest AI-driven rise in UK productivity growth," the Bank said. Even industries supposedly best placed to benefit from the technology have little to boast about. Productivity growth has improved in AI-heavy sectors such as information and communications, but has yet to exceed pre-pandemic averages. That's not to say AI isn't doing anything for the British economy. The bank estimates that AI-related activity has accounted for just under a fifth of UK GDP growth since the beginning of 2026, though much of that appears to come from companies developing and deploying the technology rather than businesses becoming more productive by using it. "The contribution to growth from AI to date appears to reflect activity in the upstream development and implementation of AI technologies rather than broader gains from their adoption elsewhere in the economy," the report said. In other words, selling AI is proving rather more lucrative than actually using it, The bank also cautioned against giving AI too much credit for Britain's recent productivity improvements. Much of the increase appears to reflect businesses hiring fewer workers while output continues to grow, partly as companies unwind post-pandemic staffing decisions and respond to higher employment costs. And despite predictions that AI will make vast swathes of the workforce redundant, firms responding to the Bank's Decision Maker Panel survey reported virtually no overall impact on employment so far. The technology is, however, making some employers less inclined to hire new staff or replace those who leave. Other studies suggest businesses are still waiting for the payoff. A Gartner survey published last month found that while three-quarters of corporate board members expected AI to improve productivity and cut costs, just 3 percent of organizations had actually achieved their targets. Meanwhile, 38 percent were already over budget on AI spending, yet 85 percent planned to spend even more next year. Another study involving nearly 6,000 executives , published in February, found that more than 80 percent of firms had seen no discernible impact from AI on either employment or productivity. Apparently, the answer to disappointing returns is to keep writing checks. That growing disconnect between AI spending and actual returns has also caught the attention of financial watchdogs. The International Monetary Fund warned last month that the AI spending spree could come back to bite investors if the promised profits don't show up, potentially dragging the wider economy down with it. The Bank for International Settlements sounded a similar alarm in June , comparing the current spending spree to the dotcom boom of the 1990s. Its concern is that tech giants are committing enormous sums to infrastructure on the assumption that AI will eventually deliver equally enormous returns, leaving them exposed if reality fails to cooperate. However, AI is already making its presence felt in one area: prices. The Bank of England noted that surging demand for AI-related products, including memory chips, has pushed up export prices in China and other Asian economies, raising import costs for Britain. So while businesses are still waiting for their AI-powered productivity windfall, the costs of the boom are already making their way through the economy. The bank isn't writing off the technology just yet. Businesses surveyed expect AI to add around 0.9 percentage points to annual productivity growth over the next three years, with the gains split roughly equally between faster output growth and slower employment growth. It seems the AI industry's most impressive productivity achievement is convincing businesses to keep opening their wallets. ®

title: Britain's tech ambitions depend on minerals made in China, MPs warn
zh_title: 议员警告称，英国的科技雄心依赖于中国制造的矿物
summary: 英国对人工智能、先进芯片和清洁能源的雄心依赖于中国主导的矿产供应链，议员们表示，他们无法确定部长们是否有可靠的计划来减少这种依赖。下议院商业、创新、科学和贸易委员会为部长们设定了十项测试，以确保关键矿物的安全。它的裁决并不乐观——它不能确信政府会通过其中任何一项。这些测试涵盖部长们是否知道哪些行业和技术需要保护、他们需要哪些矿物、哪些地方的供应可能会受到干扰，以及国内如何保护这些产业和技术。
content:
英国对人工智能、先进芯片和清洁能源的雄心依赖于中国主导的矿产供应链，议员们表示，他们无法确定部长们是否有可靠的计划来减少这种依赖。下议院商业、创新、科学和贸易委员会为部长们设定了十项测试，以确保关键矿物的安全。它的裁决并不乐观——它不能确信政府会通过其中任何一项。这些测试涵盖部长们是否知道哪些行业和技术需要保护、需要哪些矿产、哪些地方的供应可能会受到干扰，以及国内生产、海外合作伙伴关系、技能和融资将如何缩小差距。在今天发布的一份报告中，该委员会警告说，供应多样化将需要 10 到 15 年的时间，并且需要持续的投资以及与盟友的合作。报告称，将中国完全排除在外既不现实也不可取。让北京拥有如此大的影响力则是另一回事。关键矿物支撑着从电池和半导体到数据中心和军事设备的一切。该称号反映了它们的经济或安全重要性以及对供应中断的脆弱性，而不是一个特别独特的地质俱乐部的成员资格。英国与包括美国、欧盟、日本和印度在内的几乎所有主要工业化经济体一样，几乎完全依赖这些材料和矿产品的进口。
但在中国境外开采更多矿石只能解决部分问题。更大的瓶颈是加工。该委员会援引国际能源署的数据称，中国是 20 种战略矿产中 19 种的领先炼油国，平均市场份额为 70%。矿井上方的不同旗帜并不一定意味着通过炼油厂的路线不同。暴露的范围不仅仅限于芯片和电池。正如《The Register》八月份报道的那样，铒用于放大光纤链路中的信号，而钇则用于陶瓷电容器等组件。 IEEE Spectrum 警告说，中国实际上垄断了制造商所需的工业可用材料的加工。这种集中已经造成了破坏。中国于 2025 年 4 月在美国征收关税后实施稀土出口管制，波及制造业供应链，并迫使汽车工厂临时关闭。即使英国不是预定目标，英国制造商也可能遭受损失。该委员会还重点介绍了用于雷达、通信和电子战的先进半导体的镓和锗。报告显示，中国的产量分别占全球的 95% 和 93%。北京在芯片材料方面发挥影响力并不新鲜。随着西方对半导体技术的限制收紧，中国于 2023 年 7 月宣布了镓和锗的出口许可要求。
然而议员们表示，政府尚未明确确定要保护哪些国内工业和技术能力，因此很难确定哪些供应链值得优先考虑。进口统计数据也没有揭示全部风险。矿物质可能会进入电池、磁铁和其他制造部件内部，并作为单独的材料从视野中消失。企业本身可能并不确切地知道其供应链中的几层到底是什么。该委员会希望与c中的公司进行保密的映射和压力测试

【原文 English Original】
Britain's ambitions for AI, advanced chips, and clean energy rest on mineral supply chains dominated by China, and MPs say they cannot establish whether ministers have a credible plan to reduce that dependence. The House of Commons Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Committee has set ministers ten tests for securing critical minerals. Its verdict is hardly glowing – it cannot be confident the government passes any of them. The tests cover whether ministers know which industries and technologies need protecting, what minerals they require, where supplies could be disrupted, and how domestic production, overseas partnerships, skills, and financing will close the gaps. In a report published today , the committee warns that diversifying supplies will take ten to 15 years, and will require sustained investment and cooperation with allies. Completely cutting China out is neither realistic nor desirable, it says. Leaving Beijing with so much leverage is another matter. Critical minerals underpin everything from batteries and semiconductors to datacenters and military equipment. The designation reflects their economic or security importance and vulnerability to supply disruption, rather than membership of an especially exclusive geological club. The UK – like pretty much all major industrialized economies including the US, the EU, Japan, and India – is almost entirely dependent on imports of these materials and mineral product s. But digging up more ore outside China would solve only part of the problem. The bigger bottleneck is processing. Citing International Energy Agency figures, the committee says China is the leading refiner for 19 of 20 strategic minerals, with an average market share of 70 percent. A different flag over the mine does not necessarily mean a different route through the refinery. The exposure extends beyond chips and batteries. As The Register reported in August , erbium is used to amplify signals in fiber-optic links, while yttrium goes into components including ceramic capacitors. IEEE Spectrum warned that China effectively monopolized the processing of both into the industrially usable materials manufacturers need. That concentration has already caused disruption. China's rare earth export controls in April 2025 , introduced following US tariffs, rippled through manufacturing supply chains and forced temporary automotive plant closures. British manufacturers can suffer even when Britain isn't the intended target. The committee also highlights gallium and germanium, used in advanced semiconductors for radar, communications, and electronic warfare. China accounts for 95 percent and 93 percent of their global production respectively, according to the report [PDF]. Beijing flexing its leverage over chip materials is not new. China announced export licensing requirements for gallium and germanium in July 2023 amid tightening Western restrictions on semiconductor technology. Yet MPs say the government has not clearly identified which domestic industrial and technological capabilities it wants to protect, making it difficult to determine which supply chains deserve priority. Nor do import statistics reveal the whole exposure. Minerals can arrive inside batteries, magnets, and other manufactured components, disappearing from view as individual materials. Businesses themselves may not know precisely what lies several layers down their supply chains. The committee wants confidential mapping and stress-testing with firms in critical sectors, followed by joint purchasing arrangements with allies to give new mining and refining projects dependable customers. Committee chair Liam Byrne said: "Critical minerals are the alpha of the new economy. We cannot re-arm Britain, build AI or deliver net zero unless we secure the minerals these technologies depend on. "Yet sixteen years after China first weaponised its chokehold over rare earths , Britain remains dangerously exposed. We don't know enough about what minerals we need or where to find them. Our energy costs make processing uneconomic, we're exporting valuable metal waste, and our public finance institutions are shackled by outdated rules." More than a shopping list The committee's five-part prescription is to identify the capabilities Britain must protect, map their mineral needs, expand domestic mining, processing, and recycling, pool purchasing power with allies, and establish a dedicated financing facility. The proposed facility would bring together public funding bodies to back projects through grants, equity, loans, guarantees, and long-term purchase agreements. "We're never going to eliminate Chinese minerals from our supply chains. But it's foolish to leave Britain exposed to economic coercion when we could be building alternative supplies," Byrne said. "That's why we need a new Critical Minerals Finance Facility with the financial firepower to invest in new mines, processing plants and recycling, working with our allies to share the costs." The report argues that existing institutions leave gaps, particularly for early-stage projects. It recommends expanding UK Export Finance's remit and allowing British International Investment to take equity stakes in overseas mineral projects. Long-term purchasing commitments and price guarantees could help keep strategically important projects commercially viable despite volatile mineral prices. There is also material closer to home. The report says 80 percent of UK metal products classified as waste are exported. MPs want better sorting and separation infrastructure, alongside more detailed trade data to establish exactly what valuable scrap is leaving the country. For domestic projects, they recommend designated critical mineral clusters with permitting deadlines, help navigating approvals, energy support, and priority grid access. Stockpiles could provide a short-term buffer too. The committee calls for an initial reserve covering approximately 60 days of minerals needed for defense capabilities, while stressing that warehouses are no substitute for diversified supply. None of this offers a quick escape from dependence on China. The committee's argument is that Britain needs to decide what it must protect, work out what those industries actually consume, and help finance alternatives before the next disruption. "De-risking even a prudent proportion of our supplies will take over a decade. Britain cannot afford to drift," Byrne said. "We must act now before dangerous dependencies become strategic liabilities." ®

title: Nvidia tightens tracking of AI GPUs in Southeast Asia as Chinese chip smuggling draws scrutiny, report claims
zh_title: 报告称，随着中国芯片走私受到审查，英伟达加强了对东南亚人工智能 GPU 的追踪
summary: 据报道，东南亚计算提供商如果想成为官方 Nvidia 云合作伙伴（NCP），现在必须在 Nvidia 的舰队情报跟踪系统中注册。据彭博社报道，此举旨在为这家芯片制造商提供另一种方式来监控其人工智能加速器的部署位置，因为华盛顿对受限制的硬件通过区域走私网络进入中国越来越感到沮丧。未能立即联系到英伟达置评。深入了解 TH Premium：台湾、贸易和关税（图片来源：tsmc）
content:
据报道，东南亚计算提供商如果想成为官方 Nvidia 云合作伙伴（NCP），现在必须在 Nvidia 的舰队情报跟踪系统中注册。据彭博社报道，此举旨在为这家芯片制造商提供另一种方式来监控其人工智能加速器的部署位置，因为华盛顿对受限制的硬件通过区域走私网络进入中国越来越感到沮丧。未能立即联系到英伟达置评。深入了解 TH Premium：台湾、贸易和关税（图片来源：tsmc） 虽然美国在芯片制裁上反复无常，但中国正在建立自己的芯片供应市场 中国长达十年的半导体发展状况 华为 Ascend NPU 路线图审查了中国长鑫存储的目标，到 2030 年，第六座大型晶圆厂将占据 30% 的 DRAM 内存市场份额 中国最新一轮稀土出口管制解释 NCP 称号值得追求，因为它为云提供商提供了机会英伟达的公众认可和优先使用其广受欢迎的人工智能芯片，使该公司能够利用这些优势作为杠杆。据熟悉新要求的人士透露，寻求这一资格的客户现在必须注册 Fleet Intelligence。车队管理于去年 12 月推出，主要作为数据中心管理工具。它收集有关参与公司基础设施中部署的 NVIDIA 硬件的信息，包括各个加速器的位置。
这些信息可以让英伟达更好地了解其芯片在离开供应链后是否仍在运行。然而，该系统是一项普遍的跟踪任务。在 NCP 要求之外，参与仍然是自愿的，Nvidia 不会自动接收来自每个使用该软件的客户的位置数据。该公司还没有澄清现有的云合作伙伴是否必须注册才能保留其指定，或者该要求最终是否会扩展到东南亚以外。值得注意的是，英伟达一段时间以来一直在开发一种定位人工智能的方法。去年 12 月，我们报道称该公司开发了基于软件的 GPU 跟踪，使用 GPU 遥测和网络延迟测量来估计处理器的运行位置。英伟达将该软件描述为客户安装的代理，用于监控硬件健康状况、完整性和库存。除了数据维护之外，该技术还有明显的用途。美国限制中国公司未经许可购买先进的人工智能加速器，但当局认为价值数十亿美元的硬件已通过第三方网络到达中国买家手中，东南亚成为这些交易的重要中转站。 C4ADS 的一项调查此前已确定了将受限制的加工商转移到中国的几条路线，包括通过研究计划、空壳公司进行采购以及通过其他东南亚国家运送。
该非营利组织审查了 2022 年至 2025 年间的交易，发现通过区域贸易路线流通的价值 1,340 万美元的 Nvidia A100、H100 和 AD102 系列 GPU。其报告还将 46 亿美元的硬件采购与总部位于新加坡的 Megaspeed International 联系起来。对于英伟达来说，Megaspeed 已经成为一个特别尴尬的案例，该公司因涉嫌芯片转移而受到美国和新加坡的调查一年多了。上周，英伟达首席执行官黄仁勋为自己与该公司的交易进行了辩护，

【原文 English Original】
Southeast Asia computing providers are now reportedly required to register with Nvidia's Fleet Intelligence tracking system if they want to become official Nvidia Cloud Partners (NCPs). The move, according to Bloomberg , is aimed at giving the chipmaker another way to monitor where its AI accelerators are deployed, as Washington grows increasingly frustrated with restricted hardware finding its way into China through regional smuggling networks. Nvidia was not immediately available for comment. Go deeper with TH Premium: Taiwan, trade, and tariffs (Image credit: tsmc) While the U.S. flip-flops on chip sanctions, China is building its own chip supply market The state of China's decade-long semiconductor push Huawei Ascend NPU roadmap examined China's CXMT targets 30% DRAM memory market share by 2030 with sixth mega-fab China's latest round of rare-earth export controls explained The NCP designation is worth pursuing as it gives cloud providers Nvidia's public endorsement and preferred access to its sought-after AI chips, putting the company in a position to use those benefits as leverage. Customers seeking the status must now enroll in Fleet Intelligence , according to people familiar with the new requirements. Fleet Management was introduced last December primarily as a data centre management tool. It gathers information about NVIDIA hardware deployed across participating companies' infrastructure, including the locations of individual accelerators. That information could give Nvidia a better picture of whether its chips are operating after they leave the supply chain. The system is, however, a universal tracking mandate. Participation has remained voluntary outside the NCP requirement, and Nvidia does not automatically receive location data from every customer using the software. The company has also not clarified whether existing Cloud Partners will have to enroll to retain their designation or whether the requirement will eventually extend beyond Southeast Asia. Notably, Nvidia has been developing a way to locate AI for some time now. Last December, we reported that the company had developed software-based GPU tracking , using GPU telemetry and network latency measurements to estimate where processors are operating. Nvidia described the software as a customer-installed agent for monitoring hardware health, integrity and inventory. The technology has an obvious use beyond data maintenance. The U.S. restricts Chinese companies from purchasing advanced AI accelerators without a license, yet authorities believe billions of dollars worth of the hardware have reached Chinese buyers through third-party networks, with Southeast Asia becoming an important transit point for those transactions. A C4ADS investigation has previously identified several routes used to move restricted processors into China, including purchases through research initiatives, shell companies and shipments routed through other Southeast Asian countries. The nonprofit examined transactions between 2022 and 2025 and identified $13.4 million worth of Nvidia A100, H100, and AD102-series GPUs moving through regional trade routes. Its report also linked $4.6 billion in hardware purchases to Singapore-based Megaspeed International. Megaspeed has become a particularly awkward case for Nvidia, with the company being under U.S. and Singaporean investigation for more than a year over suspected chip diversion. Last week, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang defended his dealings with the firm, describing them as “completely normal,” adding, “we’ve studied all their deployments of our GPUs and counted every one.” Megaspeed denied any wrongdoing. In April, Megaspeed’s Malysisan data centre landlord terminated its contract, reallocating 68.4 megawatts of capacity to another cloud provider Moreover, Megaspeed is not the only example of how difficult it can be to police the movement of AI hardware. Earlier this year, U.S. prosecutors accused people associated with Super Micro of helping divert around $2.5 billion worth of Nvidia-powered servers to China through Southeast Asian intermediaries. The alleged scheme involved falsified paperwork and dummy server shells, with genuine hardware shipped onward after inspections. More recently, the company has faced additional scrutiny over its export compliance after inspections. Nvidia has also reportedly removed half of the Asian companies on its pre-approved buyer list and told cloud providers to keep at least 51% of their computing services with customers outside China.

title: 'Permanent, serious' dialogue needed with China on AI: tech-focused lawmaker
