36. Evacuation of Meibomian Glands, Using Heat Delivered Through Wearable, Open-Eye Eyelid Treatment Devices and Manual Gland Expression, Bilateral CPT 0563T (APC 5501)
CPT code 0563T describes evacuation of meibomian glands, using heat delivered through wearable, open-eye eyelid treatment devices and manual gland expression, bilateral. TearCare® is a technology-enabled interventional therapy for meibomian gland disease (MGD) and dry eye disease (DED) that continuously heats all four eyelids to a therapeutic temperature to melt or liquefy hardened oil obstructions in the meibomian glands, followed by physician-performed manual evacuation of the glands.
DED is a chronic affliction of the ocular surface. In the human eye, meibum, aqueous, and mucus form the three layers of tear film, which is the fluid that keeps the eye moist and serves the critical function of protecting the cornea. Meibomian glands are important oil producing glands located within each of the four eyelids. When healthy, these glands produce a clear liquid oil called meibum, which is expressed with every blink, coats the tear with oil, and prevents the tear from evaporating prematurely and exposing the cornea. In patients with MGD, the meibomian glands become diseased and inflamed and the meibum hardens. Obstructed meibomian glands cannot produce healthy new liquid meibum, leaving the tear uncoated and resulting in accelerated tear evaporation and an exposed cornea. This evaporative cascade is the leading cause of dry eye disease.
In the 2027 ASC/OPPS proposed rule, we proposed to continue to assign CPT code 0563T to status indicator “Q1” and APC 5733 (Level 3 Minor Procedures) with proposed payment rate of $66.91.
We received several public comments related to our proposal. The following is a summary of the comments we received.
Comments: The commenters requested that we reassign CPT code 0563T from APC 5733 to APC 5503 (Level 3 Extraocular, Repair and Plastic Eye Procedures) with status indicator “J1” and proposed payment rate of $2,808.31. They stated that they do not believe that the current assignment appropriately reflects either the clinical nature of the procedure or the resources required to furnish it. TearCare® requires specialized capital equipment, single-use bilateral treatment components, treatment of all four eyelids, clinical staff and treatment-room resources, followed by physician-performed manual evacuation of the meibomian glands. The single-use treatment components alone have a cost ( printed page 70408) that substantially exceeds the proposed APC 5733 payment.
They also pointed out that TearCare® is performed predominantly in the physician-office setting, where utilization does not generate an OPPS facility claim. Therefore, the limited HOPD claims reflect where TearCare® is currently performed rather than the resources required to furnish the procedure. They stated they do not believe these limited claims provide a representative basis for determining the appropriate APC assignment for CPT 0563T and those limited claims could have been filed in error. This is particularly important because the current APC payment, in their opinion, does not adequately recognize the resources required to furnish the procedure in the HOPD and may create a barrier for providers seeking to offer TearCare® to Medicare beneficiaries in other settings of care.
According to one of the commenters, the procedure requires dedicated equipment (SmartHub); bilateral, single-use Smartlid devices, a tool to clear glands, and additional supplies; in addition to clinical labor time for pre-service, intraservice, and post-service activities involving approximately 60 minutes. Based on these costs, the estimated hospital resource costs to perform the procedure will exceed $1,800 per procedure.
Response: We appreciate the commenters' input. We agree with the commenters that a family of APCs that describe Extraocular Procedures is more clinically appropriate for CPT code 0563T. However, because there has only been minimal claims data since CY 2020, (only 2 single claims in CY 2023 and CY 2025 final rules) and there are only 2 single claims and 3 total claims for this procedure in the claims available for ratesetting in this final rule, we concluded that the data doesn't support a payment increase of around $2,520.00. Therefore, we are assigning CPT code 0563T to Level 1 Extraocular, Repair and Plastic Eye Procedures for CY 2027.
In summary, after consideration of the public comments we received, we are not adopting our proposal as final. 37. Application of Rigid Total Contact Leg Cast, CPT Code 29445 (APC 5102)
CPT code 29445 describes a procedure of applying a Total Contact Leg Cast. Total contact casting (“TCC”—which is pressure offloading) is an integral part of the standard of care for diabetic foot ulcer (DFU) management, alongside with vascular management, infection management, and sharp debridement, deemed as the “VIPS” of DFU care. The use of TCC is often associated with higher healing rates, faster healing times, lower infection rates, and fewer amputations.
TCC is commonly applied after a debridement or grafting procedure during the same office or clinic visit to protect the wound site from ongoing pressure, which could further delay healing.
In the CY 2027 ASC/OPPS proposed rule, we proposed to continue to assign CPT code 29445 to status indicator “T” (Procedure or service, multiple procedure reduction applies; with a separate APC payment under OPPS) and APC 5102 (Level 2 Strapping and Cast Application) with proposed payment rate of $331.21.
At the August 24, 2026, HOP Panel Meeting, a presenter advised the Panel to request that CMS reassign CPT code 29445 ( Application of rigid total contact leg cast) to status indicator “S” (Procedure or Service, Not Discounted When Multiple; with a separate APC payment under OPPS). Based on the information presented at the meeting, the Panel recommended that CMS make that reassignment.
We received one comment related to CPT code 29445.
Comment: The commenter stated that CPT coding guidance allows for debridement (CPT codes 11042-11047, 97597-97598) as well as the application of CTPs (CPT codes 15271-15278) on the same date of service as the application of TCC (CPT code 29445). The cast improves the ability of the wound to heal. If a wound debridement is performed (CPT codes 11042-11047, 97597-97598), any primary or secondary dressing materials used to cover the wound would be included in the debridement and would not be separately reported. However, a TCC is not considered a wound dressing and is not included in the debridement procedure. Therefore, the cast application should be coded in addition to the code for the appropriate level of debridement, if performed, and should be assigned to status indicator “S” because the application of a TCC is labor intensive and the cost of the product is not insignificant.
Response: We thank the commenter for their input. Per our evaluation of the service and an input from our medical advisors, we determined that there are other clinical procedures that involve an application of cast, such as an application of short leg cast, described by CPT code 29405 or an Unna boot that ( printed page 70409) is also used for leg ulcer treatment, that is described by CPT code 29580, that are assigned to status indicator “T”. Therefore, we believe that status indicator “T” is appropriately assigned to TCC. As a result, we are maintaining our status indicator assignment as proposed for CY 2027.
We refer readers to Addendum D1 to this final rule with comment period for the SI meanings for all codes reported under the OPPS. Addendum D1 is available via the internet on the CMS website.

40. Fusion of Foot Bones, CPT Code 28740 (APC 5114)
CPT code 28740 (Arthrodesis, midtarsal or tarsometatarsal, single joint) describes the fusion of foot bones. In the CY 2027 OPPS/ASC proposed rule, we proposed to continue to assign CPT code 28740 to APC 5114 (Level 4 Musculoskeletal Procedures) with a status indicator of “J1” (Hospital Part B Services Paid Through a Comprehensive APC; Paid under OPPS) and proposed payment rate of $8,566.15.
We received a public comment on this proposal. The following is a summary of the comment we received and our response.
Comment: A commenter stated that the assignment of CPT code 28740 to APC 5114 may represent a violation of the 2 times rule, which may impede access to care for beneficiaries. The commenter recommended that CMS consider a volume threshold of 500 single major claims (or the existing greater or equal to 99 claims that ( printed page 70410) constitute greater than or equal to the 2 percent criterion) as the standard for designating an item or service “significant” for purposes of the 2 times rule. The commenter requested that we reassign CPT code 28740 to APC 5114 (Level 5 Musculoskeletal Procedures) to resolve the alleged 2 times rule violation.
Response: We appreciate the commenter's input. As discussed in section III.B. of this final rule with comment period, for purposes of reviewing APCs for determining violations of the two-times rule, we consider a procedure code cost significant when it has more than 1,000 single-major claims or when it has more than 99 single major claims and accounts for at least 2 percent of the single major claims used to establish the APC cost.
Based on our review of the updated claims data available for this final rule with comment period, CPT code 28740 has a geometric mean cost of approximately $12,571 based on 549 single claims. However, these claims do not meet the 2 percent threshold of claims used to establish ratesetting for APC 5114. Therefore, CPT code 28740 does not meet the significance threshold used in our evaluation of the two-times rule. The lowest-cost significant procedure in APC 5114 has a geometric mean cost of approximately $5,862.49, while the highest-cost significant procedure has a geometric mean cost of approximately $10,510.96. Consequently, we did not identify a violation of the two-times rule for APC 5114.
After consideration of the public comment, we are finalizing our proposal without modification to assign CPT code 28740 to APC 5114 with status indicator “J1” for CY 2027. The final CY 2027 payment rates for this code can be found in Addendum B to this final rule with comment period. In addition, we refer readers to Addendum D1 to this final rule with comment period for the status indicator definitions for all codes reported under the OPPS. Addenda B and D1 are available via the internet on the CMS website.

45. Insertion of Endobronchial Valves, CPT Code 31647 (APC 5155)

Comment: Commenters recommended that CMS reassign CPT code 31647 from APC 5155 to New Technology APC 1575 (New Technology—Level 38 ($10,001-$15,000)). The commenters noted that the cost of the procedure exceeds the payment by approximately $3,000 and expressed concern that this discrepancy would result in patient access to the procedure being limited, particularly considering that the alternatives for severe emphysema patients involve much more invasive and expensive treatment options. The commenter also stated that they considered an alternative clinical APC but could not identify a clinically and resource cohesive clinical APC into which to move it. The commenter stated that with no appropriate or higher clinical APC to use as an alternative, CMS should assign the procedure to a new technology APC that more closely aligns with its GMC. The commenter concluded that APC 1575 is the appropriate new technology APC for the service given that the GMC for CPT code 31647 has been in the $11,000-$12,000 range for the past 4 plus years and the GMC is $11,456 in the 2025 claims data that CMS released. Another commenter stated that the GMC for 31647 has remained consistently high over multiple years and outpatient claims are likely to remain steady, ranging from 72 to 88 claims. The commenter noted that the concern is underscored by the fact that the lowest geometric mean cost of a significant procedure in APC 5155 for CY 2027 is $5,481. The commenter stated that CMS previously received a recommendation from the HOP panel suggesting reassignment of CPT 31647 to New Tech APC 1575 and the commenter supports that recommendation as an interim measure until a permanent APC solution can be established.
Response: As recognized by one of the commenters, APC 5155 does not currently have a 2 times rule violation in the final rule data, and APC 5155 appears to be the best clinical fit for CPT code 31647 of any existing clinical APC.

In summary, after consideration of the public comments we received, we are finalizing our proposal without modification to assign CPT code 31647 to APC 5 (Level 5 Airway Endoscopy).

We received public comments on this proposal. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment: Commenters requested that we not finalize the proposed APC and status indicator assignments for CPT code 97610. The manufacturer of the UltraMIST System, which may be described by CPT code 97610, requested that CMS revise the status indicator from “Q1” to “T” and the APC assignment from APC 5051 (Level 1 Skin Procedures) to APC 5052 (Level 2 Skin Procedures). The UltraMIST System consists of a wand that delivers low-frequency ultrasound energy through a fine, sterile saline mist without touching the wound directly. Regarding the status indicator request, the manufacturer requested that we revise the status indicator to “T” for CY 2027 based on a crosswalk to CPT code 97597, which the commenter claimed was the closest clinical sibling of CPT code 97610. The commenter explained that the proposed status indicator assignment of Q1 would exclude most of the code's claims for ratesetting, since 54 percent of the claims for CPT code 97610 are total frequency claims, and therefore represent claims where the CPT code 97610 is billed alongside another service. Another commenter requested that assign CPT code 97610 to status indicator “S” to allow for more accurate claims collection specific to the service.
Regarding the proposed APC assignment, commenters requested that we revise the APC assignment for CPT code 97610 from APC 5051 to APC 5052 to better align resource use and costs to more comparable wound treatment codes, like CPT codes 97610 (Negative pressure wound therapy, (eg, vacuum assisted drainage collection), utilizing disposable, non-durable medical equipment including provision of exudate management collection system, topical application(s), wound assessment, and instructions for ongoing care, per session; total wound(s) surface area less than or equal to 50 square centimeters) and 97608 (Negative pressure wound therapy, (eg, vacuum assisted drainage collection), utilizing disposable, non-durable medical equipment including provision of exudate management collection system, topical application(s), wound assessment, and instructions for ongoing care, per session; total wound(s) surface area greater than 50 square centimeters), which we proposed to assign to APC 5052.
Response: We thank the commenters for their feedback. Regarding the status indicator for CPT code 97610, we believe that a crosswalk to the status indicator for a debridement service as recommended by commenters ( e.g. CPT code 97597, which is assigned to status indicator “T”), is appropriate in terms of clinical and resource similarity. Regarding the APC assignment for CPT code 97610, while we acknowledge that the service is often provided at the same time as other procedures, we note that the $196.40 geometric mean cost based on the 3,778 single frequency claims aligns closely with the geometric mean cost of the proposed APC 5051, which is approximately $221. Therefore, we are declining to finalize a revised APC assignment for CPT code 97610 and will continue to evaluate the claims data in future years.
In summary, after consideration of the public comments we received, we are finalizing our proposals with modifications. Specifically, we are finalizing a revised status indicator of “T” for CPT code 97610 and finalizing assignment of CPT code 97610 to APC 5051 as proposed. Refer to Table 46 for the code descriptor, APC assignment, and status indicator assignment for CPT code 97610 for CY 2027.

We received public comments on this proposal. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment: Several commenters requested that CMS reassign CPT code 95846 from APC 5722 (Level 2 Diagnostic Tests and Related Services) to a higher-level APC. Commenters stated that the high-complexity service requires more sophisticated equipment and supplies, additional physiologic sensors and channels, greater software and data processing capabilities, and additional technical resources.

Commenters requested that CMS assign CPT codes 95844 and 95846 to separate APCs and consider available cost information and other supporting evidence in determining the appropriate APC assignments. A commenter specifically requested that CMS reassign CPT code 95846 to APC 5723 (Level 3 Diagnostic Tests and Related Services), while maintaining CPT code 95844 in APC 5722. After consideration of the public comments and further review of the clinical and resource characteristics of CPT code 95486, we agree with the commenters that CPT code 95486 should be assigned to a higher-level APC than CPT code 95844. We believe that the greater number of channels and physiologic parameters associated with the high-complexity unattended sleep study described by CPT code 95486, as well as the additional equipment, supplies, and technical resources associated with furnishing the service, support assignment to APC 5723 (Level 3 Diagnostic Tests and Related Services). We believe that APC 5723 more appropriately reflects the clinical and resource characteristics of the service.
Therefore, after consideration of the public comments we received, we are finalizing with modification our proposal and assigning CPT code 95846 to APC 5723 (Level 3 Diagnostic Tests and Related Services) with status indicator “S” for CY 2027. We will continue to monitor the claims data for these new codes as the data become available and reevaluate their APC assignments in future rulemaking, as appropriate.
The final CY 2027 payment rates for these codes can be found in Addendum B to this final rule with comment period. 53. Digital Mental Health Treatment (DMHT) Services, HCPCS Code G0552 (APC 5012)
HCPCS code G0552 (Supply of digital mental health treatment device and initial education and onboarding, per course of treatment that augments a behavioral therapy plan) describes the supply of a digital mental health treatment device and initial patient education and onboarding. HCPCS code G0552 is currently assigned to APC 5012 (Clinic Visits and Related Services), with a proposed CY 2027 payment of approximately $148, and a status indicator of `V' (Clinic or Emergency Department Visit).
We received public comments on this proposal. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our response.
Comment: Commenters requested that CMS reconsider the proposed assignment of HCPCS code G0552 (Supply of digital mental health treatment device and initial education and onboarding, per course of treatment that augments a behavioral therapy plan) to APC 5012 (Clinic Visits and Related Services). Commenters stated that the assignment of HCPCS code G0552 to APC 5012 does not appropriately reflect the clinical characteristics or hospital resources associated with furnishing a DMHT device.
Commenters stated that HCPCS code G0552 differs from remote physiologic monitoring (RPM) and remote therapeutic monitoring (RTM) services assigned to APC 5012 because HCPCS code G0552 includes the supply of an FDA-authorized digital treatment device in addition to initial education and onboarding. Commenters explained that DMHT devices deliver a therapeutic intervention to treat or alleviate a mental health condition, whereas RPM and RTM devices generally monitor a patient's status or response to treatment. Commenters also stated that the device supply for HCPCS code G0552 is furnished for an entire course of treatment, rather than being separately reported on a recurring basis.
Commenters further stated that the hospital costs associated with furnishing DMHT devices substantially exceed the payment rate for APC 5012. Commenters also stated that CMS's proposed payment policy for Software as a Medical Service (SaMS) supports recognizing hospital expenditures for access to proprietary software as a resource cost under the OPPS, even though DMHT devices are not included within the proposed definition of SaMS.
Commenters recommended that CMS reassign HCPCS code G0552 to a higher-paying APC that more appropriately reflects the clinical and resource characteristics of the service. One commenter suggested APC 5735 (Level 5 Minor Procedures) or APC 5723 (Level 3 Diagnostic Tests and Related Services), or, alternatively, the establishment of a new Level 4 Health and Behavioral Services APC 5824.
Response: We thank the commenters for their recommendations and the information provided regarding the clinical characteristics and costs associated with furnishing DMHT devices. We continue to believe that APC 5012 (Clinic Visits and Related Services) is the most appropriate APC assignment for HCPCS code G0552 at this time. As discussed in in the CY 2025 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (89 FR 94087 through 94088), we believe that the DMHT services described by HCPCS codes G0552, G0553, and G0554 are clinically similar to other services assigned to APC 5012, and we believe that maintaining these services within the same APC continues to be appropriate based on the information currently available to us.
We acknowledge the commenters' concerns regarding the costs associated with the DMHT device included in HCPCS code G0552 and appreciate the additional cost information submitted by the commenters. However, we do not believe that the information submitted provides a sufficient basis at this time to reassign HCPCS code G0552 to APC 5723 or APC 5735, or to establish a new Level 4 Health and Behavioral Services APC.
As additional claims data become available for HCPCS code G0552, we will continue to evaluate the clinical and resource characteristics of the service and consider whether a different APC assignment may be appropriate in future rulemaking. Therefore, after consideration of the public comments, we are finalizing our proposal to continue to assign HCPCS code G0552 to APC 5012 (Clinic Visits and Related Services) for CY 2027.

55. Cystourethroscopy With Lithotripsy and Vacuum Aspiration of Kidney, HCPCS Codes C9761 and C0814 (APCs 5375 and 5376)
HCPCS code C9761 ( Cystourethroscopy, with ureteroscopy and/or pyeloscopy, with lithotripsy, and ureteral catheterization for steerable vacuum aspiration of the kidney, collecting system, ureter, bladder, and urethra if necessary, with use of steerable ureteral catheter or suction-integrated ureteroscope) became effective October 1, 2020 and describes a minimally invasive procedure used to break up and remove kidney stone fragments and dust by use of a continuous irrigation and vacuum system. The long descriptor was revised in CY 2023 to include “must use a steerable ureteral catheter” and we further revised the long descriptor to include “suction-integrated ureteroscope” effective July 1, 2026, after meeting with the specialty society.
We also established HCPCS code C8014 (Cystourethroscopy, with ureteroscopy and/or pyeloscopy, with lithotripsy, including use of a suction enabled ureteral access sheath, with irrigation (if performed) effective July 1, 2026, to describe these cystourethroscopy procedures where a suction-enabled ureteral access sheath is used to vacuum kidney stone fragments. We assigned HCPCS code C8014 to APC 5375 (Level 5 Urology and Related Procedures) and status indicator `J1' as we believe this procedure with this device has clinical and resource similarities to other procedures assigned to APC 5375.
For CY 2027, the OPPS payment rates are proposed based on available CY 2025 claims data. For the CY 2027 proposed rule, we found a total of 3,516 single frequency claims and a geometric mean cost of approximately $9,472 for HCPCS code C9761. For CY 2027, we proposed to maintain the APC assignment of 5376 (Level 6 Urology and Related Procedures) and status indicator of `J1' for HCPCS code C9761.
For CY 2027, we proposed to maintain the APC and status indicator assignment for HCPCS code C8014. We currently have no claims data for ratesetting purposes as this is a new code.
We received public comments on these two HCPCS codes. Below is a summary of the comments and our responses.
Comment: A commenter suggested that we consolidate both C-codes into one single technology-neutral code to describe suction-assisted ureteroscopic and/or pyeloscopic lithotripsy and if we did not consolidate the two C-codes, provide exclusive coding instructions for each of these HCPCS codes. The commenter explained that both of these C-codes describe suction-assisted stone-fragment evacuation during cystourethroscopy with ureteroscopy and/or pyeloscopy with lithotripsy and are furnished during the same procedure, through the same anatomic pathway, and for the same purpose. The commenter believes the device distinction is not enough of a meaningful difference to require separate HCPCS codes or have a different APC assignment. The commenter cites studies supporting their position that the performance between a flexible and navigable suction access sheath (FANS) and the CVAC system described by C9761. The commenter then went on to say that if CMS continues to maintain both HCPCS codes, C9761 and C8014 should be assigned to the same APC. The commenter requested that CMS publish clear coding instructions with illustrative examples distinguishing between the three types of devices: (1) a suction-enabled ureteral access sheath ( i.e., FANS); (2) a steerable vacuum-aspiration ureteral catheter ( i.e., CVAC system); and (3) a suction-integrated ureteroscope noting that additional coding guidance would support accurate coding and reduce claims denials.
Another commenter requested that we reassign C8014 to APC 5376 (Level 6 Urology and Related Services stating that the reassignment would be more appropriate, both clinically and based on resource utilization. The commenter noted that there are a number of complex kidney stone procedures in APC 5376, including HCPCS code C9761. The commenter believes that because we do not yet have claims data available for C8014 for our standard geometric mean cost (GMC) methodology, clinical coherence with existing APC assignments should receive significant consideration in evaluating the appropriate APC placement, such as C9761 as a crosswalk. In addition, the commenter provided their analysis of claims data to support their belief that C8014 would be more appropriately assigned to APC 5376.
Another commenter supported the creation of HCPCS code C8014 and its APC assignment to APC 5375 (Level 5 Urology and Related Services). They believe that the creation of this code will help CMS measure utilization, resources, and costs separately from the service described by HCPCS code C9761 ( printed page 70418) and refine payment as we begin to have claims data.
The commenter expressed concerns regarding the revised long descriptor for C9761 stating that the revised language causes some further confusion with cases involving a suction-capable ureteroscope (also commonly referred to as a direct in-scope suction (DISS) ureteroscope), with or without a suction-enabled ureteral access sheath. The commenter requested clarification regarding the term “integrated” and suggested that there be a documentation-based framework that articulates three different care pathways to distinguish the type of technology used (or not used), including (1) the standard ureteroscopy/lithotripsy pathway; (2) the suction-enabled access sheath pathway; and (3) the steerable-vacuum aspiration pathway. The commenter states that the clinical literature does not support the equivalency of suction-capable ureteroscopes and suction-enabled access sheaths are equivalent to the steerable renal vacuum-aspiration service represented by HCPCS code C9761.
This commenter believes that our coding clarification should distinguish the device predicate from the service predicate and further clarification is necessary for payment accuracy, beneficiary protection, and program integrity. The commenter suggests that HCPCS C9761 is coded when the services actually provided are less resource intensive. To remedy these concerns, the commenter requested that CMS issue provider communication explaining the three types of care pathways to distinguish the types of technology used and define “suction-integrated ureteroscope” in functional terms, or in the alternative, revise the current long descriptors to provide clarity regarding the service described by the code.
Response: We appreciate the input and recommendations from the interested parties. Over the years we have heard from interested parties regarding concerns about providers utilizing HCPCS code C9761 to describe the ureteroscopy/lithotripsy procedure with a suction-enabled ureteral access sheath and the potential program integrity concerns that raises when C9761 is assigned to a higher APC because of the underlying device costs. To remedy these concerns, we created C8014 to specifically describe the ureteroscopy/lithotripsy procedures with suction-enabled sheaths and assigned it to what we believe is an appropriate APC. We then heard from the American Urological Association who then informed us that there is a third type of device (suction-integrated ureteroscope) that is used to vacuum stone fragments during ureteroscopy/lithotripsy procedures. As a result, we revised the descriptor language to include this device in the descriptor for C9761.
We do not believe that we should at this time consolidate these two HCPCS codes into one single technology neutral code and assign it to APC 5376. While we understand the rationale, we do not want to create further coding confusion since we just created C8014 to distinguish suction-enabled sheaths from steerable vacuum catheters and suction-integrated ureteroscopes. We believe the descriptor language is clear and that there is enough of a difference in costs that warrants separate coding. In addition, we do not believe both HCPCS codes should be assigned to the same APC.
In response to the comments regarding coding guidance and MLN education, we have stated in past rules that we do not provide coding guidance, as it is out of scope for the OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (89 FR 94122) and if hospitals have questions about appropriate coding that they cannot resolve on their own, the appropriate first step would be to review the HCPCS codes or consult their Medicare Administrative Contractor (MAC) for their jurisdiction. We refer readers to MLN Matters MM14477 (OPPS July 2026 Update) for information regarding the creation of C8014 and the descriptor revision for C9761.
In summary, after consideration of the public comments we received, we are finalizing our proposal without modification, to assign HCPCS code C9761 to APC 5376 (Level 6 Urology and Related Procedures) and a status indicator of `J1' and HCPCS code C8014 to APC 5375 (Level 5 Urology and Related Procedures) and a status indicator of `J1'. As we do every year, we will monitor the claims data and reevaluate the APC assignments for these codes in the next rulemaking cycle to determine if more appropriate APC assignments are warranted.
The final CY 2027 payment rates for these codes can be found in Addendum B to this final rule with comment period. In addition, we refer readers to Addendum D1 to this final rule with comment period for the status indicator definitions for all codes reported under the OPPS. Addenda B and D1 are available via the internet on the CMS website.

57. Permanent Prostatic Urethral Stent, CPT Code 52282 (APC 5375)
The ProVee® System is indicated to treat obstructive lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS) secondary to benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) in men with prostatic urethral lengths greater than or equal to 3.75 cm and prostatic volumes between 30 cc and 80 cc. The insertion of a permanent prostatic urethral stent procedure, represented by CPT code ( printed page 70419) 52282 (Cystourethroscopy, with insertion of permanent urethral stent), became effective January 1, 1998, and describes the insertion of a permanent urethra stent using an endoscope. This procedure offers another therapy option for select patients with lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS) secondary to BPH.
For CY 2026, we assigned CPT code 52282 to APC 5374 (Level 4 Urology and Related Services) with a payment rate of $3,601.33 based on its geometric mean cost of approximately $3,775, which was calculated using the available 115 single frequency claims from the CY 2024 claims data.
For the CY 2027 OPPS/ASC proposed rule, we reviewed the CY 2025 claims submitted between January 1, 2025 through December 31, 2025, that were processed on or before December 31, 2025, for CPT code 52282 and found 109 single frequency claims available for ratesetting, with a resulting geometric mean cost of $4,005 (91 FR 41810). We noted that there has not been an FDA authorized permanent prostatic urethral stent on the US market for approximately 9 years until a permanent prostatic urethral stent received their FDA PMA approval in late 2025. Therefore, we believed the report claims for CPT code 52282 did not accurately represent the device and service cost associated with inserting a permanent prostatic urethral stent. Based on our examination of device and service costs associated with a permanent prostatic urethral stent, we believed it was appropriate to move CPT code 52282 to APC 5375 (Level 5 Urology and Related Services) from APC 5374 (Level 4 Urology and Related Services) because CPT code 52282 shares more resource cost and clinical homogeneity with procedures in APC 5375. Specifically, we believed CPT code 52282 shares resource and clinical homogeneity with HCPCS code C9739 (Cystourethroscopy, with insertion of transprostatic implant; 1 to 3 implants). Therefore, for CY 2027, we proposed to reassign CPT code 52282 from APC 5374 (Level 4 Urology and Related Services) to APC 5375 (Level 5 Urology and Related Services) (91 FR 41810).
Comment: We received twelve comments on our proposal. Two commenters supported our proposal to move CPT code 52282 from APC 5374 to 5375. 10 commenters requested that we move CPT code 52282 to APC 5376 (Level 6 Urology and Related Services). Some of these commenters additionally requested device-intensive status for CPT 52282. IV. OPPS Payment for Devices
A. Pass-Through Payment for Devices
1. Beginning Eligibility Date for Device Pass-Through Status and Quarterly Expiration of Device Pass-Through Payments
The intent of transitional device pass-through payment, as implemented at 42 CFR 419.66, is to facilitate access for beneficiaries to the advantages of new and truly innovative devices by allowing for adequate payment for these new devices while the necessary cost data is collected to include the costs for these devices into the procedure APC rate (66 FR 55861). Under section 1833(t)(6)(B)(iii) of the Act, OPPS transitional pass-through payment status for a device category are limited to a period of not less than 2 years but not more than 3 years.
In the CY 2017 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period, in accordance with section 1833(t)(6)(B)(iii)(II) of the Act, we amended § 419.66(g) to provide that the pass-through eligibility period for a device category begins on the first date on which pass-through payment is made under the OPPS for any medical device described by such category (81 ( printed page 70424) FR 79654). In addition, in the CY 2017 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period, we finalized a policy to allow for quarterly expiration of pass-through payment status for devices to afford a pass-through payment period that is as close to a full 3 years as possible for all pass-through payment devices (81 FR 79655). We also established a policy to package the costs of the devices that are no longer eligible for pass-through payments into the costs of the procedures with which the devices are reported in the claims data used to set the payment rates (67 FR 66763). We refer readers to the CY 2017 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (81 FR 79648 through 79661) for a full discussion of the current device pass-through payment policy.[23]
b. Expiration of Transitional Pass-Through Payments for Certain Devices
As stated earlier, section 1833(t)(6)(B)(iii) of the Act requires that, under the OPPS, a category of devices be eligible for transitional pass-through payments for at least 2 years, but not more than 3 years. Currently, 21 device categories are eligible for pass-through payment. These devices are listed in Table 49, previously published as Table 29 of the CY 2027 OPPS/ASC proposed rule (91 FR 41815 through 41816), where we detail the expiration dates of pass-through payment status for each of the 21 devices currently receiving device pass-through payment.
2. New Device Pass-Through Applications for CY 2027
Section 1833(t)(6) of the Act provides pass-through payments for devices, and section 1833(t)(6)(B) of the Act requires CMS to use categories to determine the eligibility of devices for pass-through payments. As part of implementing the statute through regulations, we continue to believe that pass-through payments for devices that offer substantial clinical improvement are important to ensure that hospitals can provide Medicare beneficiaries with access to the advantages of the new technology. Conversely, we have noted that the need for additional payments for devices that offer little or no clinical improvement over previously existing devices is less apparent. In such cases, these devices can still be used by hospitals, and hospitals will be paid for them through appropriate APC payment. Moreover, a goal is to target pass-through payments for devices where cost considerations are most likely to interfere with patient ( printed page 70426) access (66 FR 55852; 67 FR 66782; and 70 FR 68629).
As specified in regulations at § 419.66(b)(1) through (3), to be eligible for transitional pass-through payment under the OPPS, a device must meet the following criteria:
If required by FDA, the device must have received FDA approval or clearance (except for a device that has received an FDA investigational device exemption (IDE) and has been classified as a Category B device by FDA), or meet another appropriate FDA exemption; and the pass-through payment application must be submitted within 3 years from the date of the initial FDA marketing authorization, if required, unless there is a documented, verifiable delay in U.S. market availability after FDA marketing authorization is granted, in which case CMS will consider the pass-through payment application if it is submitted within 3 years from the date of market availability;
The device is determined to be reasonable and necessary for the diagnosis or treatment of an illness or injury or to improve the functioning of a malformed body part, as required by section 1862(a)(1)(A) of the Act; and
The device is an integral part of the service furnished, is used for one patient only, comes in contact with human tissue, and is surgically implanted or inserted (either permanently or temporarily), or applied in or on a wound or other skin lesion.
As finalized in CY 2026 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period, skin substitutes with an approved Biologics License Application (BLA) will be considered under transitional drug pass-through payment status, and skin substitutes with FDA Premarket approval (PMA) or FDA 510(k) clearance will continue to be evaluated under transitional device pass-through payment status (90 FR 53636).
In addition, according to § 419.66(b)(4), a device is not eligible to be considered for device pass-through payment if it is any of the following: (1) equipment, an instrument, apparatus, implement, or item of this type for which depreciation and financing expenses are recovered as depreciable assets as defined in Chapter 1 of the Medicare Provider Reimbursement Manual (CMS Pub. 15-1); or (2) a material or supply furnished incident to a service (for example, a suture, customized surgical kit, or clip, other than a radiological site marker).
Separately, we use the following criteria, under § 419.66(c), to determine whether a new category of pass-through payment devices should be established. The device to be included in the new category must—
Not be appropriately described by an existing category or by any category previously in effect established for transitional pass-through payments, and was not being paid for as an outpatient service as of December 31, 1996;
Have an average cost that is not “insignificant” relative to the payment amount for the procedure or service with which the device is associated as determined under § 419.66(d) by demonstrating: (1) the estimated average reasonable cost of devices in the category exceeds 25 percent of the applicable APC payment amount for the service related to the category of devices; (2) the estimated average reasonable cost of the devices in the category exceeds the cost of the device-related portion of the APC payment amount for the related service by at least 25 percent; and (3) the difference between the estimated average reasonable cost of the devices in the category and the portion of the APC payment amount for the device exceeds 10 percent of the APC payment amount for the related service (with the exception of brachytherapy and temperature-monitored cryoablation, which are exempt from the cost requirements as specified at § 419.66(c)(3) and (e)).
To meet the cost criterion for device pass-through payment status, a device must pass all three tests of the cost criterion for at least one APC. We generally use the lowest APC payment rate applicable for use with the nominated device when we assess whether a device meets the cost significance criterion, thus increasing the probability the device will pass the cost significance test (69 FR 65775), and we calculate the device offset amount at the HCPCS/CPT code level (81 FR 79657); and
Demonstrate a substantial clinical improvement, that is, the device to be included in the category has demonstrated that it will substantially improve the diagnosis or treatment of an illness or injury or improve the functioning of a malformed body part compared to the benefits of a device or devices in a previously established category or other available treatment, or, for devices for which pass-through payment status will begin on or after January 1, 2020, as an alternative pathway to demonstrating substantial clinical improvement, a device is part of the FDA's Breakthrough Devices Program and has received marketing authorization for the indication covered by the Breakthrough Device designation.
In the CY 2016 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period, we changed our device pass-through evaluation and determination process. Device pass-through applications are still submitted to CMS through the quarterly process, but the applications are subject to notice and comment rulemaking in the next applicable OPPS annual rulemaking cycle. Under this process, all applications preliminarily approved during quarterly review will automatically be included in the next applicable OPPS annual rulemaking cycle, while applicants whose submissions are not approved during quarterly review will have the option of being included in the next applicable OPPS annual rulemaking cycle or withdrawing their application from consideration. Under this notice-and-comment process, applicants may submit new evidence, such as clinical trial results published in a peer-reviewed journal or other materials, for consideration during the public comment process for the proposed rule. This process allows those applications that we are able to determine meet all of the criteria for device pass-through payment under the quarterly review process to receive timely pass-through payment status, while still allowing for a transparent, public review process for all applications (80 FR 70417 through 70418).
In the CY 2023 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period, we finalized our policy to publicly post online OPPS device pass-through applications received on or after March 1, 2023, beginning with the issuance of the CY 2025 OPPS/ASC proposed rule and for each OPPS rulemaking thereafter. We refer readers to the CY 2023 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period (87 FR 71934 through 71938) for a full discussion of the policy to publicly post OPPS device pass-through applications.
In the CY 2020 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period, we finalized an alternative pathway for devices that are granted a Breakthrough Device designation (84 FR 61295) and receive FDA marketing authorization for the indication covered by the Breakthrough Device designation. Under this alternative pathway, devices that are granted an FDA Breakthrough Device designation are not evaluated in terms of the current substantial clinical improvement criterion at § 419.66(c)(2) for the purposes of determining device pass-through payment status but do need to meet the other requirements for pass-through payment status in our regulation at § 419.66. Devices that are part of the Breakthrough Devices Program, have received FDA marketing ( printed page 70427) authorization for the indication covered by the Breakthrough Devices designation, and meet the other criteria in the regulation can be approved through the quarterly process and announced through that process (81 FR 79655). Proposals regarding these devices and whether pass-through payment status should continue to apply are included in the next applicable OPPS rulemaking cycle.
As discussed in the FY 2027 IPPS/LTCH PPS proposed rule (91 FR 19457 through 19459), we proposed to repeal the alternative pathway for new technology add-on payment and OPPS device pass-through applications and require all applicants for new technology add-on payments and OPPS device pass-through payments to demonstrate that they meet the same eligibility requirements to receive add-on payments and/or pass-through payments. Specifically, we proposed that all applications received for OPPS device pass-through payment status on or after October 1, 2026, including all applications received through the remainder of the CY 2028 OPPS application cycle ending on March 1, 2027, and applications received for subsequent calendar years would have to demonstrate that the technology met the requirements currently reflected at § 419.66(c)(2)(i). OPPS device pass-through payment applications submitted as of September 30, 2026, for devices that are part of the FDA's Breakthrough Devices Program and received FDA marketing authorization for the indication covered by the Breakthrough Device designation would be evaluated and could be approved under the alternative pathway, provided that all other criteria have been met. Existing device category codes established based on the approval, either preliminary or via a final determination made in an OPPS/ASC final rule, including any device category codes established for approved alternative pathway applications received as of September 30, 2026, would continue to be eligible for device pass-through payment status and would remain in effect for at least 2 years, but no more than 3 years, consistent with § 419.66(g). Previously existing device category codes that were no longer eligible for device pass-through payment status would remain unchanged. We proposed to revise paragraph § 419.66(c)(2)(ii) to reflect this proposed policy. If finalized as proposed, the change would go into effect on October 1, 2026 (91 FR 19458).
In the FY 2027 IPPS/LTCH PPS final rule (91 FR 49767 through 49789; 91 FR 50346 through 50347), we finalized our policy, with modification, that, unless specifically exempted, all applications received for device pass-through payment status on or after October 1, 2026, including all applications received through the remainder of the CY 2028 application cycle ending on March 1, 2027, and applications received for subsequent calendar years will have to demonstrate that the technology met the requirements currently reflected at § 419.66(c)(2)(i).
We also finalized our policy that device pass-through payment applications submitted to CMS as of September 30, 2026, for devices that are part of the FDA's Breakthrough Devices Program that received FDA marketing authorization for the indication covered by the Breakthrough Device designation will be evaluated and could be approved under the alternative pathway, provided that all other criteria have been met. In addition, we finalized a limited exception for a new device that had received FDA Breakthrough Device designation as of September 30, 2026, and has received marketing authorization for the indication covered by the Breakthrough Device designation. Such devices will remain eligible to apply for device pass-through payment under the alternative pathway, which will continue to accept applications for CYs 2028 and 2029. As such, in order to be considered for the limited exception, CMS must receive a complete application for eligible devices under the limited exception no later than March 1, 2028.
In the FY 2027 IPPS/LTCH PPS final rule, we also finalized that existing device category codes established based on the approval, either preliminary or via a final determination made in an OPPS/ASC final rule, including any device category codes established for approved alternative pathway applications received as of September 30, 2026, will continue to be eligible for device pass-through payment status and would remain in effect for at least 2 years, but no more than 3 years, consistent with § 419.66(g). We stated that previously existing device category codes that were no longer eligible for device pass-through payment status would remain unchanged.
We finalized revisions, with modifications, to paragraph § 419.66(c)(2)(ii) to reflect the finalized policy, effective October 1, 2026.
More details on the requirements for device pass-through payment applications are included on the CMS website in the application form itself at https://www.cms.gov/​Medicare/​Medicare-Fee-for-Service-Payment/​HospitalOutpatientPPS/​passthrough_​payment.html, in the “Downloads” section.

(2) Alternative Pathway Device Pass-Through Applications
(a) Altius® Direct Electrical Nerve Stimulation System
Neuros® Medical, Inc. submitted an application for a new device category for transitional pass-through payment status for the Altius® Direct Electrical Nerve Stimulation System (the Altius® System) for CY 2027. According to the applicant, the Altius® System is an implantable neuromodulation system that provides continuous, high frequency, high amplitude nerve stimulation to either the sciatic nerve or both the tibial and common peroneal nerves by directly stimulating targeted nerves via implanted cuff electrode leads that are wrapped circumferentially around target nerves in the amputated leg. The applicant stated that the Altius® System consists of the (1) Altius® Implantable Pulse Generator (IPG), which is implanted in the abdomen; (2) Altius® Cuff Electrode Leads; (3) Altius® Battery Charger and alternating current (AC) adapter; (4) Altius® Patient Controller, which allows the patient to activate the IPG to initiate therapy; (5) Programming Wand, which is used by the provider to program and set stimulus therapy parameters; and (6) Programmer Application Personal Computer (PAPC), which includes physician programming software. The applicant is seeking a new device category for transitional pass-through payment status for only the Altius® IPG and the Altius® Cuff Electrode Lead components of the Altius® System. The applicant stated that the Altius® IPG is a rechargeable neurotransmitter device that is implanted in the abdomen and when activated, generates a continuous high frequency, high amplitude alternating current electrical stimulus (5kHz and 10kHz) via the Altius® Cuff Electrode Leads, which are circumferentially wrapped, anchored, and implanted around the nerve(s). Per the applicant, the “alternating” nature of the delivered electrical stimulus refers to the direct electrical stimulation of the circumferential electrodes within a lead distributed in an alternating fashion across these electrodes.
Table 51 provides an overview of the transitional device pass-through payment status application for the Altius® System and CMS's preliminary assessment. For additional details provided by the applicant, please refer to the online application posting available at https://mearis.cms.gov/​public/​publications/​device-ptp/​DEP250530FMCYD.
We invited public comment on whether the Altius® System meets the newness criterion at § 419.66(b)(1) and whether the Altius® IPG and the Altius® Cuff Electrode Lead components meet the eligibility criteria at § 419.66(b)(3) and (4).
We did not receive public comments regarding whether the Altius® System meets the newness criterion at § 419.66(b)(1) or whether the Altius® IPG and the Altius® Cuff Electrode Lead components meet the eligibility criteria at § 419.66(b)(3) and (4).
We received the application for device pass-through payment status for the Altius® System within 3 years of the date of FDA PMA approval. Based on our review of the application, we have determined that the Altius® System meets the newness criterion at § 419.66(b)(1) and that the Altius® IPG and the Altius® Cuff Electrode Lead components meet the eligibility criteria at § 419.66(b)(3) and (4).
In the CY 2027 OPPS/ASC proposed rule, we noted regarding the device category eligibility criterion at § 419.66(c)(1), with respect to the Altius® IPG and Altius® Cuff Electrode Lead components, that the applicant stated that no existing (current or previous) device pass-through payment categories appropriately describe the nominated device components. Per the applicant, the existing pass-through codes C1778 (Lead, neurostimulator (implantable)) and C1822 (Generator, neurostimulator (implantable), high frequency, with rechargeable battery and charging system) do not describe the Altius® IPG and the Altius® Cuff Electrode Lead components because these codes (1) are not specifically indicated for treating chronic intractable lower limb amputation pain; (2) are not capable of delivering continuous, high amplitude, high frequency alternating current; (3) do not use circumferentially wrapped and anchored cuff electrode leads to provide direct energy delivery to the targeted nerves; and (4) do not allow for physician-pre-programmed therapy delivery controlled by the patient using the patient stimulation controller. The applicant also stated that devices described by C1778 do not make direct contact with the target nerve; instead, they deliver stimulation to the general region of the pain, unlike the Altius® Cuff Electrode Leads. The applicant added that existing devices described by C1822 deliver low-amplitude, rectangular pulses per second to general or peripheral areas to increase nerve activity and produce pain relief, whereas the Altius® IPG provides continuous, high-amplitude sinusoidal waveform stimulation to decrease target nerve activity and produce on-demand pain relief. The applicant stated that the Altius® System, including the Altius® IPG and Altius® Cuff Electrode Lead components, is the only FDA-authorized neuromodulation system indicated as an aid in the management of chronic intractable phantom and residual lower limb post-amputation pain in adult amputees.
Based on the description the applicant provided, we stated that the Altius® IPG is a rechargeable neurotransmitter device that generates a continuous high frequency, high amplitude alternating electrical stimulus (5kHz and 10kHz) via the Altius® Cuff Electrode Leads, which are circumferentially wrapped, anchored, and implanted around the nerve(s), and therefore, could be appropriately described by C1778 (Lead, neurostimulator (implantable)) and C1822 (Generator, neurostimulator (implantable), high frequency, with rechargeable battery and charging system), respectively. Specifically, we stated our belief that the pass-through payment category C1778 may appropriately describe the Altius® Cuff Electrode Lead component because the pass-through payment category describes any device that is an implantable neurostimulator lead. Additionally, we stated our belief that the pass-through payment category C1822 may appropriately describe the Altius® IPG because the category includes implantable neurostimulator pulse generators that deliver high-frequency stimulation (including approximately 10 kHz) and are rechargeable using an external charging system. Further, we stated that C1822 does not describe the amplitude, pulse frequency, or waveform of the stimulation generated by the device. We noted that CMS does not establish pass-through device categories for the purpose of describing specific devices, but rather, device categories are intended to encompass all devices that can be appropriately described by a category. In this context, we stated that we believed that the Altius® IPG and the Altius® Cuff Electrode Lead components may be appropriately described by C1778 and C1822. We also stated that, after reviewing the information provided by the applicant, we were unable to determine that the Altius® System, inclusive of the Altius® IPG and the Altius® Cuff Electrode Lead components, meets the device category eligibility criteria, and therefore, we proposed to deny transitional pass-through payment status for CY 2027.
We invited public comment on whether the Altius® IPG and the Altius® Cuff Electrode Lead components meet the device category eligibility criterion at § 419.66(c)(1). We also invited public comments on our proposal to deny transitional pass-through payment status for the Altius® System, inclusive of the Altius® IPG and the Altius® Cuff Electrode Lead components for CY 2027.
Comment: A few commenters expressed their support for the denial of device pass-through payment for the Altius® System, stating that the nominated device does not meet all the criteria needed to qualify for transitional pass-through payment.
Response: We appreciate the commenters' input. We have taken these comments into consideration in our final determination for pass-through payment status for the Altius® System.
Comment: The applicant and many commenters requested that CMS approve device pass-through payment for the Altius® System. The applicant and these commenters stated that denying pass-through payment for the Altius® System would create major financial barriers for hospitals and surgical centers, resulting in fewer offering the device, and therefore, limiting Medicare patients' access to a proven, non-opioid treatment for severe post-amputation pain. In addition, the applicant and commenters stated that the Altius® System offers a meaningful safety and quality-of-life benefit, as well as directly supporting CMS and the broader public health system's ongoing priorities to expand non-opioid pain therapies.
The applicant and commenters stated that they believe there are no existing device categories or categories previously in effect that appropriately describe the Altius® System. In response to our concerns that the Altius® IPG and the Altius® Cuff Electrode Lead components may be appropriately described by C1778 and C1822, the applicant and commenters stated that, in the proposed rule, CMS misclassified the Altius® System under C codes for legacy spinal cord stimulation (SCS) and peripheral nerve stimulation (PNS) devices, specifically C1778 (Lead, neurostimulator implantable) and C1822 (generator, neurostimulator (implantable), high frequency, with rechargeable battery and charging system). The applicant and commenters stated that neither C1778 and C1822, nor any existing neurostimulator codes, adequately describe the Altius® System because it is a fundamentally new type of device. The applicant and commenters ( printed page 70432) reiterated that the Altius® System is an FDA Breakthrough-designated therapy engineered specifically to deliver an on-demand, high-frequency, high-amplitude alternating current and circumferential electric nerve conduction block.
The applicant and several commenters stated that the Altius® System represents a distinct technology class defined by a unique mechanism of action (neurostimulation that results in a complete electrical nerve block), a unique electrode design (360° circumferential cuff surgically wrapped around the sciatic nerve or its main branches through a dedicated open surgical implant), and a unique energy delivery profile (high blocking amplitude in a continuous alternating current (5-10k Hz) in 30 minute). The applicant and commenters compared the Altius® System's mechanism of action to that of legacy SCS and PNS devices which rely on percutaneous leads placed near a nerve that stimulate the nerve at a low amplitude and frequency (10-100 Hz) in discrete pulses using a field effect to produce paresthesia intended to mask pain. The applicant and commenters stated that paresthesia cannot override the constant, high-frequency ectopic firing of a damaged peripheral neuroma, eventually rendering these legacy devices ineffective. The applicant and commenters stated that the Altius® System deadens nerve endings in a completely different way than current peripheral and spinal cord stimulators, and, as a result, no existing device categories describe the nominated device and its novel therapy. The applicant and commenters further explained that implanting the Altius® Cuff Electrode Lead, a full circumferential cuff, requires an open surgical procedure under general anesthesia in an ambulatory surgical center or hospital outpatient department, rather than the quick needle-based placement used for standard leads done in office.
In addition, the applicant stated that existing OPPS Ambulatory Payment Classifications (APCs) for general neurostimulators reflect low-cost, percutaneously-inserted needle lead systems and do not cover the additional expenses associated with the Altius® System. The applicant stated that, by stating C1822 appropriately describes the Altius® IPG, CMS is equating high-frequency spinal cord generators that deliver low-amplitude pulsed direct current into the epidural space to alter central gating without blocking nerve conduction with the Altius® IPG's high-amplitude alternating current generator that produces a true peripheral nerve conduction block. According to the applicant, by stating that C1778 appropriately describes the Altius® Cuff Electrode Lead components, CMS is also equating percutaneous lead wires place adjacent to tissues with the Altius® Cuff Electrode Lead's 360-degree cuff electrode that is surgically wrapped around the sciatic nerve. The applicant concluded that grouping the Altius® IPG and the Altius® Cuff Electrode Lead components under legacy SCS and PNS codes (C1822 and C1778) mischaracterizes the Altius® System's physics, biology, and clinical reality. The applicant further suggested that CMS create the following new device category code that would appropriately describe the Altius® System: neurostimulator system, peripheral, circumferential nerve block, includes an implanted rechargeable pulse generator (high frequency, high amplitude, alternating current), implanted cuff electrode(s) (wrapped around nerve), and patient controller.
Another commenter stated that the existing HCPCS device categories, including C1778 and C1822 appropriately describe the Altius® System and its components. The commenter stated that, as CMS noted, C1822 does not describe a specific amplitude, pulse frequency, or waveform generated by a device. The commenter stated that rather, HCPCS device categories are intended to encompass all devices that share the relevant functional and technological characteristics, not to distinguish among individual products based on proprietary design features. Further, the commenter stated that the Altius® System's lead design does not appear to be sufficiently unique to warrant creation of a new device category. Per the commenter, other commercially available neurostimulation systems utilize leads that wrap around and anchor to a target nerve. The commenter stated, for example, that LivaNova's VNS TherapyTM System employs a helical lead that coils around the vagus nerve and is secured in place, demonstrating that circumferential nerve-wrapping lead designs are already present in the market and can be appropriately accommodated within existing neurostimulator lead categories. The commenter concluded that distinctions resting on a device's approved indication, electrode geometry, stimulation parameters, control interface, or the physiologic direction of its effect do not identify anything absent from the current HCPCS framework nor is the analysis altered by Breakthrough Device Designation, which affects only the requirement to demonstrate substantial clinical improvement and does not displace the pass-through requirement at § 419.66(c)(1).
Response: We appreciate the applicant's and commenters' input. After consideration of the public comments we received and further review of the application, we agree with the applicant that there is no existing device category, or category previously in effect, that appropriately describes a neurostimulator system that uses high-frequency, alternating current.
In the proposed rule, we also invited public comment on whether the Altius® IPG and the Altius® Cuff Electrode Lead components meet the cost criterion at § 419.66(d).
We did not receive any comments regarding whether the Altius® IPG and the Altius® Cuff Electrode Lead components meet the cost significance criteria as described at § 419.66(d). Based on our findings from the first, second, and third cost significant tests, we continue to believe the Altius® IPG and the Altius® Cuff Electrode Lead components meet the cost significance criteria specified at § 419.66(d).
After consideration of the public comments we received and our review of the device pass-through application, we have determined that the Altius® System, inclusive of the Altius® IPG and the Altius® Cuff Electrode Lead components, meets the requirements for device pass-through status described at § 419.66. Therefore, we are approving the Altius® System for device pass-through payment status effective January 1, 2027, under the alternative pathway for devices that have an FDA Breakthrough Device designation and FDA marketing authorization for the indication covered by the Breakthrough Device designation.
IceCureTM Medical Ltd. submitted an application for a new device category for transitional pass-through payment status for the ProSense® Cryoablation System for CY 2027. According to the applicant, the ProSense® Cryoablation System is designed to destroy tissue by the application of extreme cold temperatures utilizing liquid nitrogen for the treatment of breast cancer for patients with low-risk tumors. The applicant stated that the ProSense® Cryoablation System is comprised of (1) the ProSense® Chassis, (2) an adjustable touch screen, and (3) external accessories, including introducers, liquid nitrogen dewar, holder, foot pedal, and Prosense® Cryoprobes. The ( printed page 70433) applicant is seeking a new device category for transitional pass-through payment status for only the ProSense® Cryoprobe component of the ProSense® Cryoablation System. Per the applicant, the ProSense® Cryoprobe is a rigid probe with a tip that creates ice balls to destroy target tissue through cycles of freezing and thawing.
Table 52 provides an overview of the transitional pass-through payment status application for the ProSense® Cryoablation System and CMS's preliminary assessment. For additional details provided by the applicant, please refer to the online application posting available at https://mearis.cms.gov/​public/​publications/​device-ptp/​DEP251226K6A1C.
We stated in the CY 2027 OPPS/ASC proposed rule that, as stated previously, with respect to the newness criterion at § 419.66(b)(1), the device must have received FDA approval or clearance (that is, FDA marketing authorization), and the pass-through payment application must be submitted within 3 years from the date of the initial FDA marketing authorization. We noted that in the CY 2016 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period, we clarified that we intended to convey that the 3-year timeframe for submitting a device pass-through payment application would be triggered by the initial FDA approval or clearance, and not by any subsequent FDA approvals or clearances. We specified “initial” FDA clearance or approval in § 419.66(b)(1) because, in some cases, FDA will provide supplemental approvals or new clearances for a device lineage after the initial approval or clearance (80 FR 70420). We further stated in the proposed rule that we received a pass-through payment status application for the ProSense® Cryoablation System on December 26, 2025, which we did not believe was within 3 years of the initial FDA marketing authorization.
We also stated in the proposed rule (91 FR 41825) that the ProSense® Cryoablation System, inclusive of the ProSense® Cryoprobe, was previously cleared on December 20, 2019, in K183213, the 510(k) clearance for the IceCure Family Cryoablation System (IceSenseTM 3, ProSense®, MultiSense).[24] We also noted that the predicate device described in K183213, the IceSenseTM 3 System, was previously cleared on November 29, 2010, in K102360,[25] and the preceding predicate device, the Galil Medical SeedNet Family, was cleared on November 18, 2005, in K052530.[26] We noted that according to K183213, cryoablation is the fundamental technological principle for both the subject IceCure Family of cryotherapy devices and the predicate IceSenseTM 3 System cleared in K102360 and the Galil Medical SeedNet Family cleared in K052530. Finally, we noted that according to K183213, the ProSense® Cryoablation System is a mere rebranding of the cleared IceSenseTM 3 single-probe system cleared in K102360, and the ProSense® Cryoablation System has the same hardware and software components as the IceSenseTM 3 System. We also noted that per K183213, the hardware and software changes introduced since the device was originally cleared on November 29, 2010, in K102360, were analyzed and determined not to require new 510(k) premarket notifications and that the K183213 submission includes the current configuration of the system.
We noted in the CY 2027 OPPS/ASC proposed rule that the October 3, 2025, FDA decision summary for De Novo classification for the ProSense® Cryoablation System includes a new indication for use in the treatment of patients with T1 invasive breast cancer and/or patients not suitable for surgical alternatives for the treatment of breast cancer. We stated that based on the information in K183213, we believed that the initial FDA marketing authorization date for the ProSense® Cryoablation System, inclusive of the nominated ProSense® Cryoprobe component, may be as early as November 18, 2005, or as recent as December 20, 2019. We stated that the applicant submitted the pass-through payment application on December 26, 2025, which was more than 3 years after either November 18, 2005, or December 20, 2019; therefore, we stated we did not believe that the ProSense® Cryoablation System, inclusive of the nominated ProSense® Cryoprobe, meets the newness criterion.
We invited public comment on whether the ProSense® Cryoablation System meets the newness criterion at § 419.66(b)(1).
Comment: A commenter expressed its support for the denial of device pass-through payment for the ProSense® Cryoablation System. ( printed page 70436)
Response: We appreciate the commenter's input.
Comment: The applicant submitted a public comment in support of device pass-through payments for the ProSense® Cryoablation System, noting that the nominated device meets all the transitional device pass-through payment criteria. The applicant also stated that transitional pass-through payment is intended to reduce financial disincentives and for new technology to be adopted so that it provides a substantial clinical improvement to Medicare beneficiaries. The applicant stated that the population for which FDA authorized the ProSense® Cryoablation System is primarily the Medicare population, and without transitional pass-through payment, hospitals face a disincentive to adopt the only FDA-authorized, non-surgical local treatment for low-risk breast cancer, particularly for women for whom surgery is an unsuitable option. In addition, the applicant stated that CMS establishing a device category effective January 1, 2027, would allow Medicare beneficiaries access to the ProSense® Cryoablation System while hospitals are making adoption decisions.
With respect to the newness criterion at § 419.66(b)(1), the applicant requested that CMS recognize October 3, 2025, as the initial date of FDA marketing authorization and the beginning of the newness period for the ProSense® Cryoablation System. The applicant reiterated that FDA granted the ProSense® Cryoablation System De Novo classification on October 3, 2025, and maintained that this is the initial date of FDA authorization for purposes of device pass-through payment status. The applicant also noted that it submitted its application for transitional pass-through payment on December 26, 2025, within three years of this date. The applicant stated that FDA classified the ProSense® Cryoablation System as a new generic device type under a newly created classification regulation (21 CFR 878.4355): cryoablation device for local treatment of low-risk breast cancer. The applicant added that FDA assigned this device type a new product code, QXW (DEN220077), consistent with section 513(f)(2) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act which states that the classification shall be the initial classification of the device.
According to the applicant, federal regulations (21 CFR 860.200(a)) state that the purpose of the De Novo process is to classify devices for which there is no legally marketed device on which to base a review of substantial equivalence. The applicant stated that because FDA granted the ProSense® Cryoablation System De Novo authorization, rather than 510(k) clearance, FDA has already determined that there is no legally marketed predicate device for the nominated device. The applicant further stated that FDA's De Novo order created a device type, a classification regulation, and a product code that did not previously exist, and it imposed special controls, including a 400-patient, 30-site post-market surveillance study, that apply to no prior cryoablation clearance. Additionally, the applicant stated that it is inappropriate for CMS to extrapolate to previous 510(k) devices when FDA has already determined that the device qualifies for De Novo classification. The applicant concluded that CMS should use October 3, 2025, as the initial date of FDA marketing authorization, and recognize that the ProSense® Cryoablation System meets the criteria for the transitional pass-through payment.
Response: We appreciate the applicant's input. After consideration of the public comments we received and our review of the application, we continue to believe that the ProSense® Cryoablation System, including the nominated Prosense® Cryoprobe, received FDA marketing authorization prior to the October 3, 2025 De Novo classification. As previously discussed, the current ProSense® Cryoablation System was included in K183213, cleared on December 20, 2019, and that clearance identified the previously cleared IceSenseTM 3 System in K102360 as its predicate. As we stated in the proposed rule, in the K183213 clearance, FDA stated that the ProSense® Cryoablation System is a rebranding of the IceSenseTM 3 single-probe system in K102360, with the same hardware and software components. Additionally, FDA stated that it analyzed and determined that the hardware and software changes introduced since the IceSenseTM 3 System clearance on November 29, 2010 did not require new 510(k) premarket notifications. The current system and cryoablation technology are traceable through FDA clearances issued on November 18, 2005 (K052530), November 29, 2010 (K102360), and December 20, 2019 (K183213). Therefore, the ProSense® Cryoablation System does not meet the newness criterion described at § 419.66(b)(1) because we received the ProSense® Cryoablation System application for device pass-through payment on December 26, 2025, which is not within 3 years of these prior FDA marketing authorizations.
While the applicant stated that the ProSense® Cryoablation System De Novo classification on October 3, 2025 established a new device type, classification regulation, and product code, and that FDA's order states that the classification is the initial classification of the device, it appears that this De Novo authorization established a new FDA classification for the device when used for the treatment of certain patients with low-risk breast cancer. Therefore, it does not constitute the initial FDA marketing authorization of this device technology for the purposes of § 419.66(b)(1), because this device technology, including the nominated cryoprobe, had previously received FDA marketing authorization with different indications for use. Although we recognize FDA's regulatory responsibility for determining the appropriate pathway for marketing authorization, CMS applies the requirements at § 419.66(b)(1) in determining whether a device technology meets the newness criterion for device pass-through payment, which does not depend on the type of FDA marketing authorization.
Because we have not received information demonstrating that the device itself is sufficiently different from the previously cleared ProSense® Cryoablation System such that October 3, 2025 should not be considered its initial FDA marketing authorization for purposes of § 419.66(b)(1), we continue to believe that the October 3, 2025, De Novo classification does not restart the newness period.
After consideration of the public comments we received and our review of the application, the ProSense® Cryoablation System does not meet the newness criterion to be considered for device pass-through payment. Therefore, in this final rule with comment period, we will not address whether the technology meets the remaining criteria required for device pass-through payment. We are not approving the ProSense® Cryoablation System for device pass-through payment status for CY 2027 because the technology does not meet the newness criterion at § 419.66(b)(1).
(c) TIDALTM Fusion Cage System (OsseraTM AFX)
Restor3d submitted an application for a new device category for transitional pass-through payment status for the TIDALTM Fusion Cage System for CY 2027. According to the applicant, the TIDALTM Fusion Cage is a single, continuous, porous piece of titanium alloy containing a circular window for an intramedullary nail used during ( printed page 70437) salvage procedures to restore bone length due to bone void, absent bone or surgical resection.
